query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are DEM contact parameters (sliding friction, rolling friction, JKR or SJKR surface energy, restitution, Young's modulus) calibrated for cohesive powders by simulating standard characterization tests: shear cells (Jenike, Schulze ring shear, FT4 rotational shear), FT4 dynamic flow (basic flowability energy), angle of repose (fixed funnel, rotating drum, lifting cylinder), Hall and Carney funnel discharge, bulk and tapped density, and uniaxial compression? Which tests are sensitive to which parameters, which parameter combinations are not identifiable from one test, and which combinations of tests break the degeneracy? Which surrogate and Bayesian methods are used (GrainLearning sequential Monte Carlo, Gaussian-process emulators, Kriging, polynomial chaos, neural-network surrogates, MCMC, approximate Bayesian computation, design of experiments), with how many simulations? Give quantitative examples for metal additive-manufacturing powders, salts and pharmaceutical powders.
task_summary: Calibrate DEM Cohesive Powder Contact Parameters Via Simulated Standard Tests And Bayesian Surrogate Methods

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.

    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

Abstract:
One of the key challenges in the implementation of discrete element method (DEM) to model powder’s flow is the appropriate selection of material parameters, where empirical approaches are mostly applied. The aim of this study is to develop an alternative systematic numerical approach that can efficiently and accurately predict the influence of different DEM parameters on various sought macroscopic responses, where, accordingly, model validation based on experimental data is applied. Therefore, design of experiment and multivariate regression analysis, using an optimized quadratic D-optimal design model and new analysis tools, i.e., adjusted response and Pareto graphs, are applied. A special focus is laid on the impact of six DEM microscopic input parameters (i.e., coefficients of static and rolling friction, coefficient of restitution, particle size, Young’s modulus and cohesion energy density) on five macroscopic output responses (i.e., angle of repose, porosity, mass flow rate, translational kinetic energy and computation time) using angle of repose tests applied to free-flowing and cohesive powders. The underlying analyses and tests show, for instance, the substantial impact of the rolling friction coefficient and the minor role of the static friction coefficient or the particle size on the angle of repose in cohesive powders. In addition, in both powders, the porosity parameter is highly influenced by the static and rolling friction coefficients.

Abstract:
The purpose of this work is to simulate the powder compaction of pharmaceutical materials at the microscopic scale in order to better understand the interplay of mechanical forces between particles, and to predict their compression profiles by controlling the microstructure. For this task, the new framework of multi-contact discrete element method (MC-DEM) was applied. In contrast to the conventional discrete element method (DEM), MC-DEM interactions between multiple contacts on the same particle are now explicitly taken into account. A new adhesive elastic-plastic multi-contact model invoking neighboring contact interaction was introduced and implemented. The uniaxial compaction of two microcrystalline cellulose grades (Avicel® PH 200 (FMC BioPolymer, Philadelphia, PA, USA) and Pharmacel® 102 (DFE Pharma, Nörten-Hardenberg, Germany) subjected to high confining conditions was studied. The objectives of these simulations were: (1) to investigate the micromechanical behavior; (2) to predict the macroscopic behavior; and (3) to develop a methodology for the calibration of the model parameters needed for the MC-DEM simulations. A two-stage calibration strategy was followed: first, the model parameters were directly measured at the micro-scale (particle level) and second, a meso-scale calibration was established between MC-DEM parameters and compression profiles of the pharmaceutical powders. The new MC-DEM framework could capture the main compressibility characteristics of pharmaceutical materials and could successfully provide predictions on compression profiles at high relative densities.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Granular materials are abundant in nature, and in most industries, either the initial constituents or final products are in granular form during a production or processing stage. Industrial processes and equipment for the handling of bulk solids can only be improved if we can understand, model and predict the material behaviour. The discrete element method (DEM) is a numerical tool well-suited for this purpose and has been used by researchers and engineers to analyse various industrial applications and processes. However, before any bulk scale modelling can be undertaken, the input parameters must be carefully calibrated to obtain accurate results. The calibration of parameter values for non-cohesive materials has reached a level of maturity; however, the calibration of cohesive materials requires more research. This paper details the most prevalent contact models used to model cohesive materials—presented in a consistent notation. Moreover, the significant differences between the models are highlighted to provide a reference for engineers and researchers to select the most appropriate model for a specific application. Finally, a critical review of calibration experiments and methodologies often used for cohesive materials is also presented. This provides a solid basis for DEM practitioners to select the most appropriate calibration methodology for their application and for researchers to extend the current state-of-the-art practices.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The lumpy zone in a blast furnace is composed of piles formed naturally during burden charging. The properties of this zone have significant effects on the blast furnace operation, including heat and mass transfer, chemical reactions and gas flow. The properties of the layers mainly include the angle of repose and porosity distribution. This paper introduces two methods, the Discharging Method and the Lifting Method, to study the influence of the packing method on the angle of repose of the pile. The relationships of the angle of repose and porosity with physical parameters are also investigated. The porosity distribution in the bottom of a pile shows a decreasing trend from the region below the apex to the center. The coordination number of the particles is employed to explain this change. The maximum of the frequency distribution of it was found to show a negative correlation to the static friction coefficient, but becomes insensitive to the parameter as the static friction coefficient increases above 0.6.

Abstract:
Laser sintering is a widely used process for producing complex shapes from particulate materials. However, understanding the complex interaction between the laser and particles is a challenge. This investigation provides new insights into the sintering process by simulating the laser source and the neck growth of particle pairs. First, a multi-physics discrete element method (DEM) framework is developed to incorporate temperature-dependent contact rheological and thermal properties, incorporating heat transfer and neck formation between the particles. Next, energy transport by ray tracing is added to allow for computing the amount of laser energy absorbed during sintering. The DEM model is calibrated and validated using experimental data on neck growth and temperature evolution of particle pairs made of polystyrene and Polyamide 12. The findings show that the proposed DEM model is capable of accurately simulate the neck growth during the laser sintering paving the way for better controlling and optimizing the process.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Micro-scale mechanisms, such as inter-particle and particle-fluid interactions, govern the behaviour of granular systems. While particle-scale simulations provide detailed insights into these interactions, their computational cost is often prohibitive. At a recent Lorentz Center Workshop on “
                    <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://www.lorentzcenter.nl/machine-learning-for-discrete-granular-media.html" ext-link-type="uri">Machine Learning for Discrete Granular Media</jats:ext-link>
                    ”, researchers explored how machine learning approaches can aid the development of constitutive laws and efficient data-driven surrogates for granular materials while also addressing uncertainty quantification. Attended by researchers from both the granular materials (GM) and machine learning (ML) communities, the workshop brought the ML community up to date with GM challenges. This position paper emerged from the workshop discussions. In this position paper, we define granular materials and identify seven key challenges that characterise their distinctive behaviour across various scales and regimes–ranging from gas-like to fluid-like and solid-like. Addressing these challenges is essential for developing robust and efficient models for the digital twinning of granular systems in various industrial applications. To showcase the potential of ML to the GM community, we present classical and emerging machine/deep learning techniques that have been, or could be, applied to granular materials. We reviewed sequence-based learning models for path-dependent constitutive behaviour, followed by encoder-decoder type models for representing high-dimensional data in reduced spaces. We then explore graph neural networks and recent advances in neural operator learning. The latter captures the emerging field evolution of interacting particles via efficient latent space representation. Lastly, we discuss model-order reduction and probabilistic learning techniques for high-dimensional parameterised systems, both of which are crucial for quantifying and incorporating uncertainties arising from physics-based and data-driven models. We present a typical workflow aimed at unifying data structures and modelling pipelines and guiding readers through the selection, training, and deployment of ML surrogates for granular material simulations. Finally, we illustrate the workflow’s practical use with two representative examples, focusing on granular materials in solid-like and fluid-like regimes.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
Calibration and validation represent crucial but often-overlooked ingredients in the successful application of discrete element method (DEM) simulations. Without rigorous calibration/validation protocols, the results of DEM simulations can be imprecise or even unphysical, yet all too often the methods used by practitioners are at best cursory, and at worst entirely absent. As the particle-handling industries show an increasing interest in DEM, it is vital that this issue be resolved lest a potentially powerful tool be written off by industry as unreliable. In this work, we provide a concise overview of contemporary methods used in the calibration and validation of DEM simulations of powder flows, providing practical insights into their strengths and weaknesses, and ideas for manners in which they may be improved and/or rendered more easily adoptable in the future.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Binder jetting of minimally processed, locally sourced sediments offers a promising route toward sustainable additive manufacturing, but powder spreading of poorly sorted, irregular grains remains underexplored. This study uses high-fidelity Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations to quantify how process parameters govern layer quality when spreading an unrefined sandy silt from the Gypsum Hills, Kansas, USA, with a counter-rotating roller. Twenty-five multi-sphere particle shapes were reconstructed from morphological measurements and used to simulate up to 300,000 interacting grains while systematically varying roller traverse speed, rotational speed, diameter, and layer thickness. Traverse speed and layer thickness emerged as the dominant controls on powder bed density and uniformity: the slowest traverse speed (20 mm/s) produced the highest density (~ 0.50) and lowest variability (~ 0.08), and layer thicknesses ≥ 120 μm were required to avoid jamming and obtain consistent packing. In contrast, roller diameter and rotational speed had only minor influence over the explored ranges. The simulations also revealed percolation-driven segregation, with fine particles preferentially settling beneath coarser grains. Comparison with an idealized spherical powder showed that the silt is intrinsically harder to spread, achieving lower density (0.51 vs. 0.59) and higher variability. These results demonstrate that binder jet processing of unrefined silt is feasible but favors slower spreading and thicker layers that may reduce throughput and resolution, and they provide process design guidelines and particle-scale insight for deploying raw earth feedstocks in sustainable binder jetting.</jats:p>

Powder bed fusion (PBF), a subset of additive manufacturing methods, is well known for its promise in the production of fully functional artefacts with high densities. The quality of the powder bed, commonly referred to as powder spreading, is a crucial determinant of the final quality of the produced artefact in the PBF process. Therefore, it is critical that we examine the factors that impact the powder spreading, notably the powder bed quality. This study utilised a newly developed testing apparatus, designed specifically for examining the quality of powder beds. The objective was to analyse the influence of various factors, including the recoater shape, recoater gap size, and the different powder flow properties, on the powder bed relative packing fraction. Additionally, the study aimed to assess the variation in the particle size and shape across the build plate. The results indicated that all of the variables examined had an impact on the relative packing fraction, as well as the size and shape variations observed across the build plate.

Abstract:
The spreading behavior of particles has a significant impact on the processing quality of additive manufacturing. Compared with spherical metal material, polymer particles are usually non-spherical in shape. However, the effects of particle shape and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, the spreading process of particles with reconstructed shapes (non-spherical particles decomposed into several spherical shapes by stereo-lithography models) are simulated by integrating spherical particles with the discrete element method. The results show that more cavities form in the spreading beds of particles with reconstructed shapes than those of spheres with blade spreading. Correspondingly, particles with reconstructed shapes have lower packing densities, leading to more uniform packing patterns. Slow propagation speeds of velocity and angular velocity lead to “right-upwards” turning boundaries for particles with reconstructed shapes and “right-downwards” turning boundaries for spherical particles. Moreover, as the blade velocity increases, the packing density decreases. Our calculation results verify each other and are in good agreement with the experiment, providing more details of the behavior of non-spherical particles before additive manufacturing. The comprehensive comparison between polymer non-spherical particles and spherical particles helps develop a reasonable map for the appropriate choice of operating parameters in real processes.

Abstract:
This paper investigates a novel approach to efficiently construct and improve surrogate models in problems with high-dimensional input and output. In this approach, the principal components and corresponding features of the high-dimensional output are first identified. For each feature, the active subspace technique is used to identify a corresponding low-dimensional subspace of the input domain; then a surrogate model is built for each feature in its corresponding active subspace. A low-dimensional adaptive learning strategy is proposed to identify training samples to improve the surrogate model. In contrast to existing adaptive learning methods that focus on a scalar output or a small number of outputs, this paper addresses adaptive learning with high-dimensional input and output, with a novel learning function that balances exploration and exploitation, i.e., considering unexplored regions and high-error regions, respectively. The adaptive learning is in terms of the active variables in the low-dimensional space, and the newly added training samples can be easily mapped back to the original space for running the expensive physics model. The proposed method is demonstrated for the numerical simulation of an additive manufacturing part, with a high-dimensional field output quantity of interest (residual stress) in the component that has spatial variability due to the stochastic nature of multiple input variables (including process variables and material properties). Various factors in the adaptive learning process are investigated, including the number of training samples, range and distribution of the adaptive training samples, contributions of various errors, and the importance of exploration versus exploitation in the learning function.

Abstract:
The kinetic characterization of the grinding process has always faced a special challenge due to the constant fluctuations of its parameters. The weight percentage of each size (WPES) should be mentioned. There are particular considerations for WPESs, because their tendencies are not monotonic. The objective of this work is to provide a methodology and model that will allow us to better understand the kinetics of grinding through the analysis of the Response Surface (RS), using geostatistical (data reconstruction) and computational intelligence (meta-model) techniques. Six experimental cases were studied and trends were evaluated/adjusted with multiple parameters, including an identity plot adjusted to 0.75–0.90, a standardized error histogram with a mean of −0.01 to −0.05 and a standard deviation of 0.63–1.2, a standardized error based on an estimated value of −0.09 to −0.02, a meta-model adjusted to between 92 and 99%, and finally, using the coefficient of variation, which classifies the information (stable/unstable). In conclusion, it was feasible to obtain the results of the WPES from RS, and it was possible to visualize the areas of greatest fluctuation, trend changes, error adjustments, and data scarcity without the need for specific experimental techniques, a coefficient analysis of the fracturing or the use of differential equation systems.

Abstract:
The discrete element method (DEM) is frequently used to investigate the behaviour of granular media (Bravo in Simulation of soil and tillage-tool interaction by the discrete element method, 2013; Tijskens et al. in J Sound Vib 266:493–514, 2003; Langston et al. in Chem Eng Sci 50:967–987, 1995; Kohring et al. in Comput Methods Appl Mech Eng 124:273–281, 1995; Stahl et al. in Granul Matter 13:417–428, 2011). The parameter calibration is a challenging task due to the large number of input parameters and the computational effort. Sometimes, this is performed with a trial-and-error approach as mentioned in Roessler et al. (Powder Technol 343:803–812, 2019), Rackl and Hanley (Powder Technol 307:73–83, 2017) based on laboratory tests, e.g. the pile experiment, the oedometer experiment and the shear test. To achieve a more suitable calibration, a better model understanding is necessary in which the influence of the DEM parameters is analysed. Consequently, the calibration can be focused on specific parameters, which have a significant influence on thef model response. If parameters with a negligibly small influence exist, the number of calibration parameters can be reduced. On this basis, it is possible to decide whether the laboratory test is suitable for the calibration of specific parameters or not. This is demonstrated with a sensitivity analysis based on Sobol’ indices for the oedometer laboratory test. In order to reduce the computational effort, the sensitivity analysis is performed with different metamodels of the oedometer simulation. The metamodels are fitted and validated with two separate sampling point sets. It is shown that the Young’s modulus for the investigated input space is the most significant parameter. This knowledge can be used to only focus the calibration on this significant parameter which enables an easier calibration and makes clear that for calibrating of other parameters this laboratory test is inappropriate. An algorithm of a force-driven plate is developed and shown which prevents non-physical states in which the interaction force between the particles and the loadplate exceeds the applied force.

Abstract:
The discrete element method and simulation analysis of the interaction between granular materials and implements provide a convenient and effective method for the optimal design of farming machinery. However, the parameter differences between different materials make discrete element simulation impossible to carry out directly. It is necessary to obtain the specific material parameters and contact parameters through parameter calibration of the simulation object, so as to make the simulation results more reliable. Parameter calibration mainly includes intrinsic parameter measurement, contact model selection, contact parameter selection, and parameter calibration. The test methods of the calibration test include the Plackett–Burman test and other methods of screening parameters with significant influence, and then selecting the optimal parameters through the climbing test, response surface analysis method, etc., and finally carrying out the regression analysis. This paper will describe the existing parameter measurement methods and parameter calibration methods and provide a reference for the scholars who study parameter calibration to carry out parameter calibration.

Abstract:
The bulk properties of powders depend on material characteristics and size of the primary particles. During storage and transportation processes in the powder processing industry, the material undergoes various modes of deformation and stress conditions, e.g., due to compression or shear. In many applications, it is important to know when powders are yielding, i.e. when they start to flow under shear; in other cases it is necessary to know how much stress is needed to keep them flowing. The measurement of powder yield and flow properties is still a challenge and will be addressed in this study. In the framework of the collaborative project T-MAPPP, a large set of shear experiments using different shear devices, namely the Jenike shear tester, the ELE direct shear tester, the Schulze ring shear tester and the FT4 powder rheometer, have been carried out on eight chemically-identical limestone powders of different particle sizes in a wide range of confining stresses. These experiments serve two goals: i) to test the reproducibility/consistency among different shear devices and testing protocols; ii) to relate the bulk behaviour to microscopic particle properties, focusing on the effect of particle size and thus inter-particle cohesion. The experiments show high repeatability for all shear devices, though some of them show more fluctuations than others. All devices provide consistent results, where the FT4 powder rheometer gives lower yield/steady state stress values, due to a different pre-shearing protocol. As expected, the bulk cohesion decreases with increasing particle size (up to 150 μm), due to the decrease of inter-particle cohesion. The bulk friction, characterized in different ways, is following a similar decreasing trend, whereas the bulk density increases with particle size in this range. Interestingly, for samples with particle sizes larger than 150 μm, the bulk cohesion increases slightly, while the bulk friction increases considerably—presumably due to particle interlocking effects—up to magnitudes comparable to those of the finest powders. Furthermore, removing the fines from the coarse powder samples reduces the bulk cohesion and bulk density, but has a negligible effect on the bulk friction. In addition to providing useful insights into the role of microscopically attractive, van der Waals, gravitational and/or compressive forces for the macroscopic bulk powder flow behaviour, the experimental data provide a robust database of cohesive and frictional fine powders for industrially relevant designs such as silos, as well as for calibration and validation of models and computer simulations.

Abstract:
Powder bed fusion additive manufacturing (PBFAM) of metals has the potential to enable new paradigms of product design, manufacturing and supply chains while accelerating the realization of new technologies in the medical, aerospace, and other industries. Currently, wider adoption of PBFAM is held back by difficulty in part qualification, high production costs and low production rates, as extensive process tuning, post‐processing, and inspection are required before a final part can be produced and deployed. Physics‐based modeling and predictive simulation of PBFAM offers the potential to advance fundamental understanding of physical mechanisms that initiate process instabilities and cause defects. In turn, these insights can help link process and feedstock parameters with resulting part and material properties, thereby predicting optimal processing conditions and inspiring the development of improved processing hardware, strategies and materials. This work presents recent developments of our research team in the modeling of metal PBFAM processes spanning length scales, namely mesoscale powder modeling, mesoscale melt pool modeling, macroscale thermo‐solid‐mechanical modeling and microstructure modeling. Ongoing work in experimental validation of these models is also summarized. In conclusion, we discuss the interplay of these individual submodels within an integrated overall modeling approach, along with future research directions.

## pqac-00000000

From text 'coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 28-30'.

Corné J. Coetzee and Otto C. Scheffler. Review: the calibration of dem parameters for the bulk modelling of cohesive materials. Processes, 11:5, Dec 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/pr11010005, doi:10.3390/pr11010005. This article has 106 citations.

The excerpt describes multi-test, multi-objective calibration rather than assigning each DEM parameter to a single independent test. For wet cohesive coal, ring-shear data at several pre-shear and shear normal pressures were used to fit particle-particle sliding friction, pull-off force, surface energy, and tensile exponent; the resulting parameter set was verified under different consolidation conditions. For cohesive iron ore, ring shear was combined with a ledge/angle-of-repose test and consolidation–penetration testing. The ledge test represented unconsolidated free flow and therefore supplied sensitivity to flow resistance, including frictional/rolling effects and cohesion. Consolidation density measured the compressed bulk state, while penetration energy represented equipment interaction and contributed additional sensitivity to stiffness and cohesive/plastic response. In the reported rotating-particle case, sliding friction, rolling friction, shear modulus (stiffness), pull-off force, surface energy, and plasticity ratio were calibrated together, with remaining values taken from literature or assumed. The excerpt does not discuss FT4 testing, restitution, Young’s modulus specifically, or JKR/SJKR identifiability. It also does not state which parameter combinations are mathematically non-identifiable from any one test; however, the use of multiple tests and multiple target values indicates that shear or angle-of-repose data alone cannot uniquely separate friction, rolling resistance, stiffness, and cohesion/surface-energy effects.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 24-28'.

Subhodh Kumar Karkala. Analysis of powder mixing and axial liquid distribution within a twin screw granulator. Text, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.7282/t3-r17v-6k57, doi:10.7282/t3-r17v-6k57. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt distinguishes calibration strategies for cohesive and non-cohesive DEM systems. For dry, free-flowing materials, angle-of-repose tests can calibrate sliding and rolling friction, and prior studies also use hopper discharge or shear-cell data; however, angle of repose may fail for highly cohesive powders because cohesive forces can prevent gravitational flow. For cohesive wet powders modeled with JKR contacts, the proposed approach uses dynamic yield strength (DYS) simulations to calibrate particle-particle surface energy, while parallel-plate shear-cell simulations calibrate particle-particle coefficients of sliding friction (CoSF) and rolling friction (CoRF). The excerpt also reports that an FT4 powder-rheometer drop test has been used to determine the JKR surface-energy parameter. It emphasizes that cohesive calibration methods are much less established than methods for cohesionless materials. The cited studies indicate that angle of repose is mainly useful for friction calibration under dry conditions, whereas DYS or drop tests are intended to identify cohesion/surface energy and shear cells target frictional parameters. This passage does not provide a calibration procedure or identifiability analysis for restitution, Young’s modulus, bulk density, or SJKR specifically, nor does it establish which combinations of those parameters are non-identifiable from a single test. Bulk density is reported as a material property rather than used here as a calibration observable.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 32-34'.

Corné J. Coetzee and Otto C. Scheffler. Review: the calibration of dem parameters for the bulk modelling of cohesive materials. Processes, 11:5, Dec 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/pr11010005, doi:10.3390/pr11010005. This article has 106 citations.

The excerpt describes a staged calibration strategy for cohesive DEM materials. First, the dry, non-cohesive parameters are calibrated using flow-property and bench-scale tests, after which cohesive parameters are introduced while the dry parameter values remain fixed. Bulk density is measured independently and compared with the simulated filled-cylinder density. Restitution is obtained from particle-particle and particle-wall drop tests, while particle-wall sliding friction is measured using Jenike direct-shear and inclined-wall tests. Young’s modulus is taken from literature or measured by nano-indentation, rather than identified from the bulk flow tests. Particle-particle sliding and rolling friction are calibrated through sensitivity studies using a swing-arm slump test and a hopper-discharge test. The same sliding friction could apply to both tests, but the tests required different rolling-friction values, indicating that friction parameters—or their combination with other parameters—are not uniquely identifiable from one test or even consistently transferable between tests. Cohesion energy density C0 is estimated from an Ajax tensile test and refined against cohesive heap-shape results. In the hopper test, cohesion had little effect on the formed repose angle but strongly affected the shear angle of material remaining in the hopper, so θR,d was used for calibration. Cohesion values inferred from the slump and hopper tests differed significantly. The excerpt does not discuss FT4 tests or provide a direct comparison with shear-cell calibration.

## pqac-00000003

From text 'roessler2019demparametercalibration pages 2-3'.

Thomas Roessler and André Katterfeld. Dem parameter calibration of cohesive bulk materials using a simple angle of repose test. Particuology, 45:105-115, Aug 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.partic.2018.08.005, doi:10.1016/j.partic.2018.08.005. This article has 213 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt distinguishes calibration tests by the bulk response they measure. Shear-cell and uniaxial-stress tests target stress behaviour and generally provide precise measurements, but require specialized equipment and careful sample preparation. Angle-of-repose or pile-surface tests target macroscopic flow behaviour and surface shape; they are simpler but less precise and more qualitative because cohesive piles can have irregular, rough surfaces. For the selected SJKR-based approach, cohesion is represented by a single cohesion energy density parameter, CJKR, with relatively low computational cost. The excerpt indicates that calibration of cohesive bulk material must consider cohesion energy density together with rolling and sliding friction coefficients. It does not provide sensitivity results for Young’s modulus, restitution, bulk density, FT4 measurements, or the separate identifiability of friction, surface energy, stiffness, and restitution from individual tests. It also warns that SJKR is unsuitable for strong consolidation and stress-history behaviour; Luding or EEPA models are more appropriate there, though they require more parameters. The paper’s proposed procedure uses a lifting-cylinder test, related to angle-of-repose-style free-surface calibration, and notes that cohesion in wet assemblies involves surface-tension and viscous effects, represented respectively through SJKR cohesion and a low coefficient of restitution.

## pqac-00000004

From text 'roessler2019demparametercalibration pages 1-2'.

Thomas Roessler and André Katterfeld. Dem parameter calibration of cohesive bulk materials using a simple angle of repose test. Particuology, 45:105-115, Aug 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.partic.2018.08.005, doi:10.1016/j.partic.2018.08.005. This article has 213 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides only a partial basis for comparing calibration tests. It explains that cohesive-material DEM calibration is difficult and that the appropriate experiment depends on the process being modeled. For a hollow-cylinder pull-up angle-of-repose test, the authors do not use only the final static angle. Instead, they evaluate macroscopic flow phases: formation of a stable column, convex bending during lifting, and the onset of collapse. Convex bending and the moment of first collapse are proposed as measurable criteria for calibrating cohesive materials, and the reported phases are independent of cylinder size and lifting velocity. Using wet sand and a simplified JKR (SJKR) cohesion model, the study selects sliding friction coefficient, rolling friction coefficient, and cohesion energy density as relevant parameters. The introduction also distinguishes cohesionless-material calibration, where rolling and sliding friction strongly affect bulk behavior, from cohesive-material calibration, which additionally requires a cohesion model. However, this excerpt does not provide results for shear cells, bulk-density tests, FT4 tests, restitution, Young’s modulus, or explicit identifiability analyses showing which parameter combinations cannot be distinguished by a single test. It therefore cannot establish the requested test-specific sensitivities or non-identifiable parameter combinations beyond indicating that experiment selection is a central calibration issue.

Abstract:
This paper presents a computational framework that generates ensemble predictive mechanics models with uncertainty quantification (UQ). We first develop a causal discovery algorithm to infer causal relations among time-history data measured during each representative volume element (RVE) simulation through a directed acyclic graph. With multiple plausible sets of causal relationships estimated from multiple RVE simulations, the predictions are propagated in the derived causal graph while using a deep neural network equipped with dropout layers as a Bayesian approximation for UQ. We select two representative numerical examples (traction-separation laws for frictional interfaces, elastoplasticity models for granular assembles) to examine the accuracy and robustness of the proposed causal discovery method for the common material law predictions in civil engineering applications.

Abstract:
Potentially habitable icy Ocean Worlds, such as Enceladus and Europa, are scientifically compelling worlds in the solar system and high-priority exploration targets. Future robotic exploration of Enceladus and Europa by in-situ missions would require a detailed understanding of the surface material and of the complex lander-surface interactions during locomotion or sampling. To date, numerical modeling approaches that provide insights into the icy terrain’s mechanical behavior have been lacking. In this work, we present a Discrete Element Model of porous planetary ice analogs that explicitly describes the microstructure and its evolution upon sintering. The model dimension is tuned following a Pareto-optimality analysis, the model parameters’ influence on the sample strength is investigated using a sensitivity analysis, and the model parameters are calibrated to experiments using a probabilistic method. The results indicate that the friction coefficient and the cohesion energy density at the particle-scale govern the macroscopic properties of the porous ice. Our model reveals a good correspondence between the macroscopic and bond strength evolutions, suggesting that the strengthening of porous ice results from the development of a large-scale network due to inter-particle bonding. This work sheds light on the multi-scale nature of the mechanics of planetary ice analogs and points to the importance of understanding surface strength evolution upon sintering to design robust robotic systems.

Abstract:
Random sampling of graph partitions under constraints has become a popular tool for evaluating legislative redistricting plans. Analysts detect partisan gerrymandering by comparing a proposed redistricting plan with an ensemble of sampled alternative plans. For successful application, sampling methods must scale to large maps with many districts, incorporate realistic legal constraints, and accurately sample from a selected target distribution. Unfortunately, most existing methods struggle in at least one of these three areas. We present a new Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithm that draws representative redistricting plans from a realistic target distribution of choice. Because it yields nearly independent samples, the SMC algorithm can efficiently explore the relevant space of redistricting plans than the existing Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms that yield dependent samples. Our algorithm can simultaneously incorporate several constraints commonly imposed in real-world redistricting problems, including equal population, compactness, and preservation of administrative boundaries. We validate the accuracy of the proposed algorithm by using a small map where all redistricting plans can be enumerated. We then apply the SMC algorithm to evaluate the partisan implications of several maps submitted by relevant parties in a recent high-profile redistricting case in the state of Pennsylvania. Open-source software is available for implementing the proposed methodology.

Abstract:
The flow behaviours of cohesive particles in the ring shear test were simulated and examined using discrete element method guided by a design of experiments methodology. A full factorial design was used as a screening design to reveal the effects of material properties of partcles. An augmented design extending the screening design to a response surface design was constructed to establish the relations between macroscopic shear stresses and particle properties. It is found that the powder flow in the shear cell can be classified into four regimes. Shear stress is found to be sensitive to particle friction coefficient, surface energy and Young’s modulus. A considerable fluctuation of shear stress is observed in high friction and low cohesion regime. In high cohesion regime, Young’s modulus appears to have a more significant effect on the shear stress at the point of incipient flow than the shear stress during the pre-shear process. The predictions from response surface designs were validated and compared with shear stresses measured from the Schulze ring shear test. It is found that simulations and experiments showed excellent agreement under a variety of consolidation conditions, which verifies the advantages and feasibility of using the proposed “Sequential Design of Simulations” approach.

Grainlearning: a bayesian uncertainty quantification toolbox for discrete and continuum numerical models of granular materials. J. Open Source Softw., 9:6338, May 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.06338, doi:10.21105/joss.06338. This article has 6 citations.

The excerpt identifies Gaussian-process regression and artificial neural networks as surrogate or meta-model approaches tested for DEM calibration. GrainLearning itself performs Bayesian calibration by combining probabilistic learning of the parameter space with iterative sampling. Its stated inference method is Sequential Monte Carlo filtering, while a variational Gaussian model learns the parameter distribution, identifies high-probability regions, and guides subsequent samples until the uncertainty tolerance is met. Calibration uses time-series reference data, parameter ranges, and a tolerance, and iteratively reduces the discrepancy between simulations and observations. The passage also mentions optimization and design-of-experiment approaches, including Latin Hypercube sampling and genetic algorithms, but says that these require too many model runs. It does not mention Kriging separately from Gaussian-process regression, polynomial chaos, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), or approximate Bayesian computation (ABC). It also gives no numerical estimate of how many simulations are typically required; it only states qualitatively that conventional optimization/design-of-experiment methods may require too many runs and that GrainLearning is intended to improve efficiency.

The workflow draws initial parameter values, runs the dynamic model, compares results with reference observations, estimates a posterior distribution through Bayesian filtering, checks convergence, and—if necessary—constructs a Gaussian mixture from the current examples to sample parameters for the next iteration. For surrogate modeling, GrainLearning can replace expensive direct DEM simulations with surrogate models such as recurrent neural networks, with the article stating that this can reduce computational cost by several orders of magnitude. The excerpt does not provide information about Gaussian-process emulators, Kriging, polynomial-chaos expansions, MCMC, or approximate Bayesian computation, nor does it state a typical or fixed number of simulations required. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11831-025-10322-8, doi:10.1007/s11831-025-10322-8. This article has 28 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies several surrogate approaches relevant to DEM-style reduced-order modelling and calibration: neural-network surrogates, polynomial response surfaces, radial-basis-function interpolation, and Gaussian-process models. It also describes Bayesian inference for estimating uncertain hidden states and model parameters from partial observations, with uncertainty propagation framed through state–parameter models containing modelling and measurement noise.                     <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Particle erosion and cavitation erosion pose persistent challenges to engineering surfaces across diverse sectors such as energy, aviation, marine, and manufacturing, frequently causing severe material degradation, operational inefficiencies, and economic losses. Surface texturing has emerged as a highly effective protection strategy, capable of significantly enhancing particle erosion and cavitation erosion resistance through near-wall flow modulation, particle impact redistribution, and mitigation of bubble collapse-induced pressure spikes. This review presents a comprehensive synthesis of recent advances in surface texturing technologies aimed at enhancing particle erosion and cavitation erosion resistance. The fundamental mechanisms governing solid particle erosion and cavitation erosion are first elucidated, followed by a comprehensive summary of theoretical frameworks for erosion–cavitation synergy and an in-depth exposition of theoretical modeling approaches for textured surfaces. Diverse surface texturing methods are systematically reviewed, with a focus on laser surface texturing, additive manufacturing-enabled micro/nano-structuring, and mechanical or hybrid surface treatments. The effects of texture geometry, scale, and arrangement on hydrodynamic flow, impact angle distribution, and stress modulation are analyzed in conjunction with substrate mechanical properties such as hardness, toughness, and residual stress. Complementary coating techniques and biomimetic morphology-material coupling strategies that synergistically enhance wear resistance and wettability are also discussed. Experimental characterization methodologies and numerical modeling approaches for performance evaluation are presented. Finally, future research directions are outlined, advocating integrated surface engineering solutions that combine texture design, material modification, and advanced modeling to optimize multi-functional resistance under complex erosive conditions.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Abstract. A comprehensive and statistically robust understanding of rock characteristics is essential for reservoir characterization of the deep subsurface to accurately plan exploration campaigns, parameterize predictive 3D geological models, interpret geophysical data, and execute numerical thermo-hydraulic-mechanical-chemical simulations, thereby reducing economic risks and project uncertainties. Despite growing interest in the crystalline basement in Germany for e.g., geothermal energy applications and the safe storage of high-radioactive nuclear waste, systematic datasets covering the major crystalline and metamorphic basement units and their physiomechanical characteristics remain scarce, fragmented, or lack the metadata required for robust evaluation. To address this data gap, the AMPEDEK project established a unified, multi-scale national reference database for geochemical, petrophysical, and mechanical rock properties of crystalline rocks in Germany. The framework integrated extensive literature reviews, data from geological surveys, and newly conducted sampling and measurement campaigns, linking metadata, geochemistry, petrography, and physiomechanical rock properties through unique sample IDs. Existing data from more than 40 studies were compiled, evaluated, and integrated into the database. In addition, approximately 650 cylindrical plugs retrieved from drill cores and outcrop samples were systematically analyzed with respect to their mineralogical, geochemical, petrophysical, and rock mechanical properties to close remaining data gaps. Particular emphasis was placed on sampling a broad spectrum of lithologies to ensure coverage of the major crystalline units in Germany. The resulting open-access repository (Weydt et al., 2026; https://doi.org/10.48328/tudatalib-2167) currently contains approximately 25,700 data points covering up to 34 parameters measured on 8,200 samples from more than 3,400 sampling locations across eight federal states in Germany. It represents the first standardized national-scale compilation of geochemical, petrophysical, and mechanical rock property data for the crystalline basement in Germany. The database provides a robust empirical foundation for early-stage exploration, reservoir characterization, and the validation of analytical measurement methods. Future efforts will focus on expanding the database towards regions with low data density and on high-temperature and high-pressure experiments to improve the understanding of parameter variations under in situ conditions.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Understanding the rheology of the Earth’s lower mantle is essential for modelling mantle convection and its consequences for the geodynamical, thermal and chemical evolution of the planet. However, the extreme pressure–temperature conditions, the long natural timescales, and the complexity of deep-mantle mineralogy make it difficult to constrain mantle viscosity from experiments alone. In this review, we examine an alternative approach based on mineral physics and multiscale numerical modelling, tracing its theoretical foundations and its development over the last decades. We first outline the key physical mechanisms governing plastic deformation in lower-mantle minerals—point defects, dislocations, diffusion, and grain-boundary processes—and the conditions under which they operate. We then summarize the major experimental advances that provide essential constraints for these models. Building on this foundation, we review the evolution of multiscale modelling strategies, from first-principles calculations of defect energetics and dislocation cores to mesoscale dislocation dynamics and polycrystal-scale formulations. Using ferropericlase and bridgmanite as archetypal examples, we show how successive developments have progressively linked atomic-scale mechanisms with macroscopic rheology under deep-mantle conditions. Finally, we discuss current limitations and outstanding challenges, including the scarcity of diffusion data at high pressures, uncertainties in defect chemistry, and the need to integrate multiphase and multimechanism deformation. Together, these elements provide a coherent view of the present capabilities of mineral-physics-based rheology and outline a roadmap for future efforts to improve our understanding of deep-mantle dynamics.</jats:p>

A multivariate regression parametric study on DEM input parameters
of free‑flowing and cohesive powders with experimental data‑based
validation

Bilal El‑Kassem1,2 · Nizar Salloum2 · Thomas Brinz2 · Yousef Heider1     · Bernd Markert1


Received: 25 September 2019 / Revised: 10 December 2019 / Accepted: 10 January 2020 / Published online: 29 January 2020
© The Author(s) 2020

Abstract
One of the key challenges in the implementation of discrete element method (DEM) to model powder’s flow is the appropri-
ate selection of material parameters, where empirical approaches are mostly applied. The aim of this study is to develop an
alternative systematic numerical approach that can efficiently and accurately predict the influence of different DEM param-
eters on various sought macroscopic responses, where, accordingly, model validation based on experimental data is applied.
Therefore, design of experiment and multivariate regression analysis, using an optimized quadratic D-optimal design model
and new analysis tools, i.e., adjusted response and Pareto graphs, are applied. A special focus is laid on the impact of six
DEM microscopic input parameters (i.e., coefficients of static and rolling friction, coefficient of restitution, particle size,
Young’s modulus and cohesion energy density) on five macroscopic output responses (i.e., angle of repose, porosity, mass
flow rate, translational kinetic energy and computation time) using angle of repose tests applied to free-flowing and cohesive
powders. The underlying analyses and tests show, for instance, the substantial impact of the rolling friction coefficient and
the minor role of the static friction coefficient or the particle size on the angle of repose in cohesive powders. In addition, in
both powders, the porosity parameter is highly influenced by the static and rolling friction coefficients.

Keywords  Discrete element method · Free-flowing powder · Cohesive powder · Design of experiment · Multivariate
regression analysis · Angle of repose

Subhodh Kumar Karkala. Analysis of powder mixing and axial liquid distribution within a twin screw granulator. Text, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.7282/t3-r17v-6k57, doi:10.7282/t3-r17v-6k57. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports parameter-sensitivity results for dynamic yield strength (DYS) and a shear-cell test, but it does not provide angle-of-repose, bulk-density, or FT4-flowability-energy results, nor does it report Sobol indices. For DYS, surface energy (corresponding broadly to cohesion energy) is the dominant parameter: increasing it from the base case produced a 274.3% increase in DYS (1853 Pa versus 495 Pa). Rolling friction was the next strongest tested effect, increasing DYS by 37.0%, while shear modulus (a possible analogue of Young’s modulus) and sliding friction reduced DYS by 19.2% and 18.8%, respectively. Poisson’s ratio and restitution were relatively insensitive, with changes of -7.7% and -4.6%. In the more detailed analysis, rolling-friction effects rose sharply up to approximately 0.30 and then weakened; sliding-friction effects were strongest from 0.01–0.40 and DYS peaked near 0.1; shear modulus had the least effect among those three. For shear-cell stress, rolling friction increased critical-state stress from 1008 to 1183 Pa when raised to 1.0, and sliding friction at 0.1 increased stress, whereas increasing it from 0.40 to 1.0 had little effect. Surface energy also affected shear-cell results, though less strongly than DYS. These findings support a qualitative ranking for DYS, not a complete ranking across all requested metrics.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>During metal binder jetting (MBJ), powder bed density critically governs binder migration and influences the final properties of the components. Heterogeneous powder bed density distribution in a single powder spreading process, possibly arising from both powder characteristics and spreading conditions, can lead to non-uniform binder saturation patterns. For process optimization in practical manufacturing, adjusting the spreading process is often more efficient than altering the powder that may have been chosen to meet final property requirements. However, the influence of process-controlled variations in powder bed density on binder migration has not yet been sufficiently addressed, and independent studies of powder spreading or binder deposition are not sufficient to capture the sequential effects. To fill this gap, this study integrated powder spreading simulations under varying spreading conditions using the discrete element method (DEM) with binder deposition simulations by computational fluid dynamics (CFD), in which the spread stainless steel 17-4PH powder beds served as the initial condition of binder deposition. The results of single-droplet simulations reveal that increasing the powder bed density initially promotes lateral binder spreading and suppresses vertical binder penetration, however, it ultimately results in a deep penetration. When extended to the more realistic multiple-droplet simulation, decreasing the droplet spacing was found to delay the local equilibrium saturation but promote the binder migration. A series of innovative single-layer printing experiments adopting the corresponding settings in the simulations confirms the validity of the developed workflow.</jats:p>
