       From Angle of Repose to Heap Morphology: Full-Field Calibration of DEM for
                                     Granular Powders


                Olivier Gaboriaulta,b, Antonella Succara, Cléo Delêtrea, Anatolie Timercanc, Roger Pelletierc, David Melanconb,
                                                    Bruno Blais1a

                 aDepartment of Chemical Engineering, High-performance Automatization Optimization and Simulation (CHAOS) laboratory, Polytechnique
                                             Montréal, 2500 Chemin de Polytechnique, Montréal, H3T 1J4, Québec, Canada
                     bDepartment of Mechanical Engineering, Laboratory for Multiscale Mechanics (LM2), Polytechnique Montréal, 2500 Chemin de
                                                             Polytechnique, Montréal, H3T 1J4, Québec, Canada
                                     cNational Research Council Canada, 75 Bd de Mortagne, Boucherville, J4B 6Y4, Québec, Canada2026
May
            Abstract
10
          The calibration of discrete element method (DEM) models is commonly performed by tuning model parameters to

           match an experimental measurements, most commonly the angle of repose (AOR). Although widely used, AOR-based

              calibration metrics do not adequately characterize the full heap morphology, particularly when dealing with cohesive

             granular materials. As a result, AOR-based calibrations often leads to non-unique parameter sets. In this work, we

            propose a DEM calibration procedure based on full-field image analysis of static powder heaps rather than scalar

        AOR measurements. The method compares an average experimental heap profile (AEHP), obtained from repeated

           GranuHeap™experiments, with an average numerical heap profile (ANHP) generated from DEM simulations. This

            comparison is performed using pixel-wise grayscale intensity values of both average heap profiles. Two metal powders[physics.app-ph]
          commonly used in additive manufacturing, Ti6Al4V and Al6061, are used to evaluate the proposed methodology. This

           work highlights the limitations of traditional AOR-based approaches and demonstrates that full-field heap morphology

              offers a more reliable framework for DEM calibration.


              1. Introduction


               Granular matter, like powders, are used for a wide range of applications. For example, in additive manufacturing,

            metal and polymer powders can be used to fabricate functional parts that are difficult or impossible to build using

             conventional manufacturing techniques [1]. In the pharmaceutical industry, powders are frequently used as part of

            drugs encapsulation and drug formulation [2]. Finally, the food industry relies heavily on the storage and processingarXiv:2605.09371v1      of granular ingredients like flour and grains. Given the widespread use of powders in industrial processes, predicting

             the performance and dynamics of granular material during their handling and manipulation is critical. In recent years,

             the discrete element method (DEM) has proven to be an efficient tool to achieve such prediction.

             The DEM is a numerical method introduced by Cundall and Strack [3] that simulates granular systems such as the

           powder spreading step for additive manufacturing [4, 5, 6, 7], granular mixers [8], fluidized beds [9] and many more.


                  1Corresponding author. Email address: bruno.blais@polymtl.ca (Bruno Blais)This method consists in tracking the position and velocity of particles over time by computing forces and torques

resulting from particle-particle and particle-wall interactions derive from different models (e.g., contact forces, sliding

friction, rolling friction, cohesive forces, etc.), requiring their own parameters (e.g., damping coefficient, sliding

friction coefficient, rolling friction coefficient, surface energy, etc.). Using these forces and torques, Newton’s second

law of motion and Euler’s law of angular motion are solved numerically for each particle using an explicit time

integration scheme. As a result, the DEM provides a high level of detail, enabling granular systems to be studied at

the particle scale, but requires substantial computational resources compared to other methods [10, 11, 12].

   When simulating granular systems, the choice of interaction models and the values of their parameters have a

drastic effect on their overall behaviour. The model parameters selection is usually achieved by comparing simulations

and experiments of small-scale test cases for the same particles. Model parameters are then tuned, manually or

automatically, to match a certain metric like the torque applied by the particle on a shaft [13] or the angle of repose

(AOR) of a static [6, 14, 15] or dynamic [4] particle heap. This calibration process has many drawbacks as it requires

a large number of tuning simulations—thus high computational resources—and does not guarantee a unique set of

model parameters. Furthermore, wall-related model parameters are often assigned constant values or simply assumed

to be equal to the particle–particle parameters, which represents a strong assumption and can introduce significant

uncertainty in the calibration process. These limitations become even more critical for cohesive powders, where

complex interparticle interactions make scalar metrics such as the AOR insufficient to fully characterize the bulk

behaviour and often lead to non-unique calibration solutions.

    In this work, we propose a novel procedure based on the image analysis of static powder heaps shapes. Rather

than relying on a scalar metric such as the AOR, the entire heap profile is used to evaluate the adequacy of a given

combination of model parameters in comparison with experimental observations. First, we introduce the calibration

procedure and assess the reproducibility of the heap experiments. Then, we present the procedure to calibrate two

metal powders used in additive manufacturing. The results of the calibration are compared with those obtained using

more traditional metrics, which rely on the AOR. We show that different clusters of calibration parameters emerge

depending on the calibration procedure and the definition of the AOR used. We conclude by discussing future work

which aims at disambiguating the parameters set in DEM simulations for cohesive powders.



2. Methodology


   The DEM calibration procedure that we introduce in this work relies on the comparison of static granular heap

profiles that are obtained experimentally and from DEM simulations. This comparison is performed using the pixel

values of two grayscale images: one representing the Average Experimental Heap Profile (AEHP) obtained from the

granular material of interest and the other representing a numerically simulated heap profile generated using a given set

of DEM model parameters. The current section first presents the powders used to demonstrate the proposed calibration

procedure, followed by the experimental methodology employed to generate the static heap, which is schematized into


                                              2a flow chart. Finally, the section conclude on the numerical framework used in our DEM simulations.


2.1. Powders

   Two powders are used in this work to demonstrate the efficacy of our calibration method. The first one is a Ti6Al4V

powder from Advanced Powders and Coatings (AP&C) while the second one is a Al6061 powder from Equispheres.

Figure 1 presents scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images and volume-based particle size distributions (PSD) for

each powder. The titanium powder present predominantly spherical particles with few satellites (Figure 1a), with a

PSD ranging from 45 to 111 µm for the 5th–95th percentile (D5-D95) (Figure 1b). The aluminium powder consists

of spherical particles with some surface texture (Figure 1c) with a PSD ranging from 18 to 50 µm for the D5-D95

(Figure 1d).

the Ti6Al4V powder from Advanced Powders and Coatings (AP&C) showing predominantly spherical particles with few satellites taken with a
NANOS tabletop SEM from Semplor at 15 kV. (b) Corresponding differential (orange) and cumulative distribution (green) of the Ti6Al4V powder
based on volume. (c) SEM image of the Al6061 powder from Equispheres showing spherical particles with some surface texture. (d) Corresponding
differential (orange) and cumulative distribution (green) of the Al6061 powder based on volume.



2.2. Experimental methodology

could be used with the proposed calibration procedure,

2.2. Experimental methodology

   The flow chart for the experimental methodology is illustrated in Figure 2. While any static heap experiment

could be used with the proposed calibration procedure, we employ a commercial device, the GranuHeap™[16], which

characterizes powder flowability through a controlled heap formation process. The device consists of a cylindrical

container filled with powder that is vertically lifted by a robotic arm at a prescribed velocity, allowing the granular


                                              3material to flow downward under gravity and form a conical heap on a base plate. As the cylinder rises, the powder

flows and reorganizes until a stable heap is obtained. For each calibration run, the heap is photographed 16 times

(Figure 2a) over a 180◦arc around the static heap. The images are binarized to clearly distinguish the heap from the

background. The relevant experimental dimensions of the apparatus, as well as the prescribed lifting velocity used in

this study, are presented in Table 1.

   The heap profile obtained with the GranuHeap is sensitive to the amount of powder used inside the cylindrical

container, up to a certain quantity. For instance, using an insufficient amount of powder results in a heap that is not

fully formed and that is highly sensitive to particle placement in the container before lifting, leading to significant

variability in the resulting heap profiles and poor repeatability between calibration experiments which is undesirable.

On the other hand, we want to limit as much as possible the amount of powder used inside our cylindrical container to

ensure that the corresponding simulations are not too computationally intensive. Indeed, an excessive powder volume

would result in a larger number of particles, thus in a higher computational cost per simulation. With this taken into

consideration, the first step of our calibration methodology is to determine the adequate amount of raw material to

use for a given powder. To do so, we repeat the GranuHeap experiment 30 times (Figure 2a-b) for predetermined

powder weights, visible in Figure 3 for each powder type. Those experiments are performed on three different days,

with 10 repetitions per day for a given powder mass, to account for environmental variability such as changes in air

humidity that can affect the powder rheology [17, 18]. For each run, an average heap profile is generated by averaging

its 16 images. In other words, the 16 binary images of a run (Figure 2a), which have pixel values that are 0 or 1,

are converted into one grayscale image (Figure 2b), which have pixel intensity values (Ip) between 0 (black) and 255

(white) inclusively. Note that black signifies the presence of powder. From these grayscale images, we compute the

4. Calibration metrics


   The angle of repose (AOR) is commonly used to calibrate DEM models [26]. Although its definition varies in

the literature depending on the application [27], it can generally be described as the angle formed between the free

surface of a granular material and the horizontal plane. Its widespread use is mainly due to its simplicity, as it can be

measured using various experimental techniques [26].

   However, this apparent simplicity also introduces challenges, particularly when dealing with cohesive powders,

which are the focus of this work. Figure 4 illustrates different methods that can be used to measure the AOR of a

cohesive powder heap. The first method is based on the ratio between the height of the heap and the radius of its

base [27] (see Figure 4a). The second and third methods both rely on a linear regression of the slope formed by the

powder heap [28, 29], but differ in the portion of the slope considered. The second methods uses the entire slope

for the linear regression, while the third method uses only the first half starting from the base (see Figures 4b-c).

Depending on the method used, the measured angle is not the same. This is not a problem in itself, provided that the

same method is consistently applied to both the experiments and the simulations. The main difficulty arises because

many different parameter combinations can yield the same AOR for a given measurement method. In other words, the

DEM parameter solution space that offers the same AOR as the experimental run is large, or is non-unique, for a given

AOR measurement method. One possible explanation for this is that the AOR does not give enough information about

the powder behaviour, especially when cohesion is non negligible. Thus, it is highly probable that the calibration of a

given cohesive powder using different AOR measurement methods, or even the same method, can lead to significantly

different parameter sets.

  A second challenge arises from the heap morphology formed by cohesive powders. The three methods illustrated

in Figure 4 implicitly assume an idealized conical heap, characterized by perfect axisymmetry and a linear free surface

profile. However, in the case of cohesive powders, these assumptions are often invalid. Consequently, the reliance on

a single geometric parameter, like the AOR, to characterize the powder heaps is not reliable.


4.1. Proposed calibration metric based on image analysis

  We propose a calibration metric based on the comparison of heap profiles using their pixel values. The first

image is the AEHP (Figure 2c), obtained from the optimum powder weight selected in Table 2. The grayscale image

associated with a given DEM calibration simulation, referred to as the average numerical heap profile (ANHP), is

generated using an in-house Paraview script that takes 16 binary images taken over a 180◦arc around the simulated

static heap and averages them. The sum of absolute differences (SAD) between the AEHP and the ANHP can then be

and 41.50◦, respectively.

ArXiv, May 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2505.02967, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2505.02967. This article has 13 citations.

The excerpt provides explicit simulation-budget information primarily for grid-based calibration. A 10 × 10 grid for two parameters requires 100 simulations, while extending the same approach to six parameters would require approximately one million simulations, illustrating the curse of dimensionality. The text also describes a design-of-experiments example for DEM calibration involving 7 microscopic parameters at 3 levels each; the excerpt does not explicitly state the resulting total number of simulations, though such a full factorial design would conventionally imply 3^7 combinations. For response-surface methodology, the passage explains that sampling points are used to fit a second-order multivariate polynomial, which is then interrogated during optimization, but it gives no fixed simulation budget. The excerpt mentions surrogate approaches, including neural networks, and discusses surrogate/metamodel calibration generally, but provides no numerical budgets for Gaussian-process surrogates or neural-network surrogates. Abstract:
An important prerequisite for the generation of realistic material behavior with the Discrete Element Method (DEM) is the correct determination of the material-specific simulation parameters. Usually, this is done in a process called calibration. One main disadvantage of classical calibration is the fact that it is a non-learning approach. This means the knowledge about the functional relationship between parameters and simulation responses does not evolve over time, and the number of necessary simulations per calibration sequence respectively per investigated material stays the same. To overcome these shortcomings, a new method called Metamodel-based Global Calibration (MBGC) is introduced. Instead of performing expensive simulation runs taking several minutes to hours of time, MBGC uses a metamodel which can be computed in fractions of a second to search for an optimal parameter set. The metamodel was trained with data from several hundred simulation runs and is able to predict simulation responses in dependence of a given parameter set with very high accuracy. To ensure usability for the calibration of a wide variety of bulk materials, the variance of particle size distributions (PSD) is included in the metamodel via parametric PSD-functions, whose parameters serve as additional input values for the metamodel.

Abstract:
When employing bonded discrete element models (DEMs) to model rocks, a fundamental problem is how to determine the micro parameters to accurately simulate the rock strength characteristics. One promising way to improve calibration efficiency is to fully utilize the underlying relationship between DEM micro parameters and the macro strengths of rocks. This paper developed an analytical-optimal calibration framework to automatically determine DEM bond strength parameters. Extensive parametric analysis was first conducted to obtain the relationships between DEM micro-parameters and macro strengths. Bond tensile strength, cohesion and local internal friction angle were identified as independent variables for calibration. The automatic calibration method is divided into two stages. Firstly, the rough estimations of the bond tensile and cohesion were obtained by successively performing a direct tensile simulation test and a uniaxial compression simulation test, while the local internal friction angle was estimated by an empirical formula about the Hoek–Brown parameter mi. In the second stage, a finite difference gradient optimization method was used to further approximate the optimal bond parameters. A simplified gradient calculation is proposed based on the sensitivity analysis of macro strengths and DEM parameters. Adaptive moment estimation (Adam) was chosen as the iterative optimization algorithm to avoid the vanishing gradient problem. The advantage of the proposed calibration method is that the relationship between macro strengths and DEM parameters is fully exploited in both the initial estimation of DEM micro parameters and the optimization process. Moreover, the optimization method is a single-solution algorithm without the need to perform a large number of numerical simulations simultaneously. The proposed framework was demonstrated by calibrating the Bukit Timah granite, and a high calibration accuracy was achieved with a few iterations and a small number of simulation runs. Its applicability was also verified by the calibration results of various types of rocks.

Abstract:
The calibration of discrete element method (DEM) simulations is typically accomplished in a trial-and-error manner. It generally lacks objectivity and is filled with uncertainties. To deal with these issues, the sequential quasi-Monte Carlo (SQMC) filter is employed as a novel approach to calibrating the DEM models of granular materials. Within the sequential Bayesian framework, the posterior probability density functions (PDFs) of micromechanical parameters, conditioned to the experimentally obtained stress–strain behavior of granular soils, are approximated by independent model trajectories. In this work, two different contact laws are employed in DEM simulations and a granular soil specimen is modeled as polydisperse packing using various numbers of spherical grains. Knowing the evolution of physical states of the material, the proposed probabilistic calibration method can recursively update the posterior PDFs in a five-dimensional parameter space based on the Bayes’ rule. Both the identified parameters and posterior PDFs are analyzed to understand the effect of grain configuration and loading conditions. Numerical predictions using parameter sets with the highest posterior probabilities agree well with the experimental results. The advantage of the SQMC filter lies in the estimation of posterior PDFs, from which the robustness of the selected contact laws, the uncertainties of the micromechanical parameters and their interactions are all analyzed. The micro–macro correlations, which are byproducts of the probabilistic calibration, are extracted to provide insights into the multiscale mechanics of dense granular materials.

## pqac-00000041

From text 'meier2021physics‐basedmodelingand pages 2-4'.

Christoph Meier, Sebastian L. Fuchs, Nils Much, Jonas Nitzler, Ryan W. Penny, Patrick M. Praegla, Sebastian D. Proell, Yushen Sun, Reimar Weissbach, Magdalena Schreter, Neil E. Hodge, A. John Hart, and Wolfgang A. Wall. Physics‐based modeling and predictive simulation of powder bed fusion additive manufacturing across length scales. GAMM-Mitteilungen, Aug 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/gamm.202100014, doi:10.1002/gamm.202100014. This article has 65 citations.

The excerpt reports one calibrated DEM parameter for the modeled metal AM powder: an effective surface energy of γ = 0.1 mJ/m², identified by fitting the simulated static angle of repose (AOR) to experiments. It emphasizes that surface energy is the most critical parameter because it can vary by several orders of magnitude with particle surface roughness, topology, and chemistry, and because it determines the particle pull-off force. For particles with mean diameter around 30 μm, the reported adhesive forces are already about an order of magnitude larger than gravity, indicating that cohesion strongly controls powder behavior. The excerpt does not provide material-specific calibrated values for Ti-6Al-4V, 316L, AlSi10Mg, or IN718, nor does it report numerical values for sliding friction, rolling friction, or the coefficient of restitution. It states that rheology tests, including static and dynamic AOR and rotating-vane tests, are used to calibrate unknown DEM parameters and assess predictive capability. Sensitivity information given here is qualitative: increasing powder cohesiveness reduces spreading quality, lowering mean packing fraction and increasing spatial variability in packing fraction and surface profile (roughness). Thus, the supplied pages support a strong sensitivity to cohesion/effective surface energy, but do not quantify sensitivities to friction or restitution.

## pqac-00000042

From text 'zhang2017machinelearningenabled pages 4-7'.

W Zhang, A Mehta, PS Desai, and CF Higgs III. Machine learning enabled powder spreading process map for metal additive manufacturing (am). Unknown journal, 2017.

The excerpt reports calibrated or assigned DEM parameters only for a virtual Ti-6Al-4V powder system; it does not provide values for 316L, AlSi10Mg, or IN718. The coefficient of restitution is listed as e = 0.8 for powder interacting with the spreader, substrate, and powder. Sliding friction coefficients are µ = 0.12 at the spreader interface, µ = 0.25 at the printed substrate interface, and µ = 0.185 for powder–powder interaction. The table notes that 0.12 was measured using a rheometer, 0.25 was assumed, and 0.185 was tuned through DEM calibration. No rolling-friction coefficient, cohesion parameter, or surface-energy value is reported in this excerpt. The methodology describes calibrating a virtual powder to behave like real AM powder, followed by DEM spreading simulations, but it does not present a parameter-sensitivity study. In particular, no quantitative sensitivity of angle of repose or powder-spreading metrics to sliding friction, rolling friction, cohesion/surface energy, or restitution is given. Spreading performance is evaluated using volume spread per unit time per unit width (Vs) and layer roughness (Rq), but the excerpt ends before reporting their dependence on DEM parameters.

## pqac-00000043

From text 'gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 9-12'.

Olivier Gaboriault, A. Succar, Cl'eo Deletre, A. Timercan, Roger Pelletier, D. Melancon, and B. Blais. From angle of repose to heap morphology: full-field calibration of dem for granular powders. ArXiv, May 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.09371, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2605.09371. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt provides only partial information relevant to the requested DEM parameters. For the calibration simulations, the authors varied tangential/sliding friction (µt,i), rolling friction (µr,i), and surface energy/cohesion (γi); the excerpt does not report their calibrated numerical values. It states that other parameters were considered less sensitive, but it does not provide a quantified sensitivity analysis for angle of repose or powder spreading. The reported restitution coefficient is 0.9 for both Ti6Al4V and Al6061. The excerpt concerns Ti6Al4V and Al6061, not 316L, AlSi10Mg, or IN718, so no values for those powders can be extracted. It also emphasizes that angle of repose alone is non-unique: different combinations of friction, rolling friction, and cohesion-related parameters can produce the same AOR. Consequently, AOR is potentially insufficient to identify powder behavior, particularly for cohesive powders. The proposed alternative is image-based comparison of experimental and simulated heap profiles using the sum of absolute pixel differences (SAD), with the lowest SAD indicating the best agreement. No specific sliding-friction, rolling-friction, surface-energy, or spreading-sensitivity results are reported in these pages.

From text 'jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 1-2'.

The excerpt identifies Young’s modulus as the parameter with the largest influence, and therefore the largest Sobol sensitivity in the investigated DEM oedometer input space. It explicitly characterizes Young’s modulus as “the most significant parameter,” indicating that it dominates the response relevant to oedometer compression and that calibration can be focused primarily on it. The study evaluates both first-order and total-order Sobol indices: first-order indices represent each parameter’s individual influence, while total-order indices also account for interactions. Rolling resistance (rolling friction) is among the parameters investigated, but the excerpt does not provide its numerical first-order or total-order sensitivity index or rank. Sliding friction is mentioned in the surrounding calibration literature, but no specific sliding-friction Sobol index or quantitative sensitivity result is given in this excerpt. Thus, the available pages support the conclusion that Young’s modulus is the dominant parameter, while they do not establish numerical sensitivity values for rolling or sliding friction. The full article’s results or figures would be needed to report those indices accurately.

The indices are plotted on a decadic logarithmic scale, so visual comparisons must account for orders of magnitude. The excerpt does not provide a textual ranking or numerical table identifying which parameter has the largest index, nor does it explicitly conclude whether Young’s modulus is the dominant parameter. It likewise does not state separate numerical sensitivity conclusions for rolling versus sliding friction. The appendix explains that first-order indices represent individual effects, while total-order indices include a parameter’s interactions with other parameters. It also states that Sobol’ indices are nonnegative and that all indices sum to one. Consequently, the figure is the relevant source for determining the leading parameter and comparing E, sliding friction, and rolling friction, but the extracted text alone is insufficient to make those comparisons reliably.

### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| DEM contact parameter | Angle of repose / heap | Shear cell (Jenike, Schulze, FT4 shear) | FT4-like dynamic yield / blade flow | Oedometer / bulk density | Powder spreading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sliding friction, μs** | **High** for free-flowing powders; **low–moderate** for cohesive powders, where rolling resistance and cohesion can dominate. Different μs–μr–γ combinations can reproduce the same angle. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000026) | **High** for pre-shear and critical-state stress; often the dominant pre-shear parameter, but sensitivity can saturate above μs ≈ 0.4. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000015) | **Moderate**; changing sliding friction produced about an 18.8% change in dynamic yield strength in one pharmaceutical-powder study. (pqac-00000015) | **High for loose packing/bulk porosity**, because μs and μr jointly control rearrangement; generally below Young’s modulus for force–displacement response in an oedometer. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046) | **Moderate–high**: controls shearing beneath the recoater and particle–substrate drag, but can trade off against rolling resistance and cohesion. A Ti-6Al-4V example used μpp = 0.185, μspreader = 0.12 and μsubstrate = 0.25. (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043) |
| **Rolling friction, μr** | **High**, especially for cohesive or spherical-particle models; commonly compensates for unresolved angularity/roughness and was the strongest AoR factor for cohesive lactose. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000018) | **Moderate–high** when particle rotation and shape interlocking matter; raising μr increased simulated critical-state stress from 1008 to 1183 Pa in one study. (pqac-00000015) | **Moderate–high**; increasing μr caused about a 37% increase in dynamic yield strength, with the strongest response up to μr ≈ 0.3. (pqac-00000015) | **High for packing/porosity** but **low relative to Young’s modulus for oedometer stiffness**. μs and μr are jointly influential and cannot usually be separated using density alone. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000044) | **Moderate–high**: governs particle rotation, apparent angularity and bed packing; however, it is confounded with μs and γ in heap-based calibration. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) |
| **JKR/SJKR surface energy, γ, or cohesion-energy density** | **High for cohesive powders**, including heap curvature, clumping, collapse onset and no-flow/bridging; a scalar AoR alone cannot uniquely separate cohesion from friction. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000025) | **High**: surface energy significantly affects pre-shear stress and was the most important factor for incipient-flow stress in a 32-run ring-shear design. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017) | **Very high**: increasing surface energy raised dynamic yield strength from 495 to 1853 Pa, a 274.3% increase, in the cited pharmaceutical example. (pqac-00000015) | **Moderate** for loose/cohesive packing, agglomeration and consolidation history; a simple elastic JKR/SJKR model is inadequate for strong irreversible compaction. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003) | **Very high for fine AM powders**: cohesion lowers mean layer packing and increases roughness/heterogeneity; for ≈30 μm metal particles, adhesion can exceed gravity by roughly an order of magnitude. (pqac-00000041) |
| **Young’s modulus / contact stiffness, E** | **Low** over many reduced-stiffness ranges, provided overlaps remain small; it can become relevant when cohesion depends on contact area. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012) | **Low for pre-shear**, but **moderate–high for incipient flow at high cohesion**; tested range 0.13–1.3 GPa. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017) | **Moderate** in the cited yield-strength study, where changing shear stiffness altered dynamic yield strength by about 19.2%; effects are model- and stress-dependent. (pqac-00000015) | **Very high for oedometer/uniaxial force–displacement response** and the dominant Sobol-sensitive parameter in the investigated oedometer domain; density alone is much less diagnostic of E. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046) | **Low–moderate** for quasi-static spreading if reduced safely; mainly controls overlap, collision/contact duration and computational time rather than final layer morphology. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) |
| **Restitution, e** | **Low–negligible** for the final static heap, though it affects transient avalanching and settling time. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000018) | **Negligible for mean pre-shear/incipient stress** in the cited screening study, but **moderate for stress-fluctuation amplitude**. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017) | **Negligible–low** under slow dense flow; changing e produced only about a 4.6% dynamic-yield-strength change in one study. (pqac-00000015) | **Low** for quasi-static density/compression after settling; principally affects collision damping rather than equilibrium stiffness. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046) | **Low–moderate**: more relevant at high recoater speed or impact-dominated deposition than in slow, dense spreading; reported AM studies often fix e rather than calibrate it. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000042) |

Rows: (1) GrainLearning Sequential Monte Carlo, (2) Kriging/Latin Hypercube Sampling, (3) Artificial Neural Network surrogate, (4) Metamodel-Based Global Calibration (symbolic regression), (5) Response Surface Methodology / D-optimal DoE, (6) Evolutionary algorithms (ACCES), (7) Full-factorial parametric sweeps. Include quantitative simulation counts from the evidence: Benvenuti 546+81 sims for iron ore, Rackl 7-parameter LHS, El-Kassem 40-53 D-optimal sims for pharmaceutical powders, Richter several hundred sims, Gaboriault 670+100 sims for Ti6Al4V/Al6061, Cheng SQMC Bayesian with iterative ensemble filtering, Chen 32 simulations for ring shear factorial."}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Method | Algorithm details | Reported / typical DEM simulation budget | Key references | Notes / advantages |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| **GrainLearning sequential Monte Carlo (SMC/SQMC)** | Runs an ensemble of parameter samples, weights trajectories by agreement with time-series observations, recursively updates the posterior, and resamples from a fitted Gaussian-mixture/variational distribution. Surrogates such as recurrent neural networks may replace DEM evaluations. | No universal count; cost is **ensemble size × calibration rounds**. In Cheng’s SQMC example, posterior changes became small after about **60 data-assimilation steps**, but these are observation increments—not 60 independent DEM runs. | Cheng et al.; GrainLearning toolbox (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030) | Produces posterior distributions and parameter correlations rather than a single optimum. Especially useful for path-dependent dosing/shear curves, but requires monitoring effective sample size, particle impoverishment, model discrepancy, and stochastic DEM variance. |
| **Kriging / Gaussian-process surrogate with Latin-hypercube sampling** | Space-filling LHS generates DEM training points; a Kriging/GP emulator maps parameters to multiple bulk responses and is searched for matching parameter sets. Predictive variance can guide adaptive sampling. | Problem-dependent. Rackl and Hanley calibrated **7 factors** against angle of repose and bulk density; the cited evidence does not give the exact run count. Conventional calibration commonly reaches **hundreds to thousands** of runs without an efficient surrogate. | Rackl & Hanley; Richter & Will (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037) | Well suited to roughly 3–8 continuous parameters and expensive DEM. Gives uncertainty estimates and exposes solution manifolds; Rackl found multiple parameter combinations with similar responses and no assumed μs–μr correlation. |
| **Artificial-neural-network surrogate** | Feed-forward ANN learns the mapping from DEM inputs to shear-cell and heap outputs; millions of candidate parameter combinations are then screened inexpensively through the trained network. | Benvenuti et al.: **546 shear-cell + 81 angle-of-repose simulations = 627 DEM runs**; the trained ANN subsequently screened **6,250,000** parameter combinations. | Benvenuti, Kloss & Pirker (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040) | Handles nonlinear, multi-output responses and makes exhaustive post-training searches cheap. Requires enough training/validation data, provides less transparent uncertainty than a GP, and can extrapolate unreliably outside the training domain. |
| **Metamodel-Based Global Calibration (MBGC; symbolic regression)** | A reusable, domain-wide surrogate is trained once across contact parameters, density, and a parameterized PSD. Symbolic regression/genetic programming seeks an interpretable global equation; later materials are calibrated without new DEM runs if they remain inside the trained domain. | **Several hundred DEM simulations** for one-time global training; subsequent calibrations can use surrogate predictions alone. | Richter & Will (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035) | Amortizes cost over many powders and yields interpretable relationships. Transfer is valid only for the same contact model, test geometry, particle representation, and covered material/PSD domain. |
| **Response-surface methodology / D-optimal design of experiments** | A screening or optimized design fits linear/quadratic regression with interactions; insignificant factors are removed and the response surface is optimized or inverted. | El-Kassem et al.: **40 runs** for free-flowing lactose and **53 runs** for cohesive lactose across five or six inputs. Chen et al.: **32 simulations** for a five-factor, two-level ring-shear screening design, followed by an augmented response-surface stage. | El-Kassem et al.; Chen, Pei & Elliott (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Efficient for screening and smooth, low-order responses; directly estimates interactions and sensitivity. Quadratic surfaces may miss discontinuities such as jamming, intermittent no-flow, avalanches, or regime changes. |
| **Evolutionary optimization (e.g., ACCES)** | Population-based evolutionary search automatically launches simulations, evaluates multiple comparators, mutates/recombines candidates, and iterates toward lower discrepancy; it can be coupled to metamodels and parallel execution. | No fixed budget in the cited evidence. Brute-force comparison shows the motivation: a 10-point grid needs **100 runs for 2 parameters** but about **1,000,000 for 6 parameters**. | Nicuşan et al. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000028) | Robust to noisy, non-smooth and multimodal objectives and easy to parallelize. Usually returns optima rather than a Bayesian posterior unless embedded in a probabilistic workflow; can still consume many DEM runs. |
| **Full-factorial / dense parametric sweep** | Evaluates every selected parameter-level combination, optionally followed by local refinement around the best candidates. It is simple and unbiased by a surrogate form but scales exponentially with dimension. | Chen ring-shear screening: **2⁵ = 32 runs**. Gaboriault et al.: **670 Ti6Al4V runs** using factorial sweep plus refinement and **100 Al6061 runs** using LHS. | Chen, Pei & Elliott; Gaboriault et al. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000026) | Provides clear interaction maps and a strong benchmark in low dimension. Becomes impractical beyond a few parameters; Gaboriault’s results also showed that different heap metrics select substantially different μs–μr–γ optima. |


*Table: Comparison of Bayesian, surrogate, optimization, and design-of-experiments strategies for DEM calibration, including reported simulation budgets. Counts are study-specific and should not be treated as universal sample-size requirements.*

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child

    Status:

        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are DEM contact parameters (sliding friction, rolling friction, JKR or SJKR surface energy, restitution, Young's modulus) calibrated for cohesive powders by simulating standard characterization tests: shear cells (Jenike, Schulze ring shear, FT4 rotational shear), FT4 dynamic flow (basic flowability energy), angle of repose (fixed funnel, rotating drum, lifting cylinder), Hall and Carney funnel discharge, bulk and tapped density, and uniaxial compression? Which tests are sensitive to which parameters, which parameter combinations are not identifiable from one test, and which combinations of tests break the degeneracy? Which surrogate and Bayesian methods are used (GrainLearning sequential Monte Carlo, Gaussian-process emulators, Kriging, polynomial chaos, neural-network surrogates, MCMC, approximate Bayesian computation, design of experiments), with how many simulations? Give quantitative examples for metal additive-manufacturing powders, salts and pharmaceutical powders.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this multi-faceted question about DEM calibration of contact parameters for cohesive powders.

Abstract:
One of the key challenges in the implementation of discrete element method (DEM) to model powder’s flow is the appropriate selection of material parameters, where empirical approaches are mostly applied. The aim of this study is to develop an alternative systematic numerical approach that can efficiently and accurately predict the influence of different DEM parameters on various sought macroscopic responses, where, accordingly, model validation based on experimental data is applied. Therefore, design of experiment and multivariate regression analysis, using an optimized quadratic D-optimal design model and new analysis tools, i.e., adjusted response and Pareto graphs, are applied. A special focus is laid on the impact of six DEM microscopic input parameters (i.e., coefficients of static and rolling friction, coefficient of restitution, particle size, Young’s modulus and cohesion energy density) on five macroscopic output responses (i.e., angle of repose, porosity, mass flow rate, translational kinetic energy and computation time) using angle of repose tests applied to free-flowing and cohesive powders. The underlying analyses and tests show, for instance, the substantial impact of the rolling friction coefficient and the minor role of the static friction coefficient or the particle size on the angle of repose in cohesive powders. In addition, in both powders, the porosity parameter is highly influenced by the static and rolling friction coefficients.

Abstract:
The purpose of this work is to simulate the powder compaction of pharmaceutical materials at the microscopic scale in order to better understand the interplay of mechanical forces between particles, and to predict their compression profiles by controlling the microstructure. For this task, the new framework of multi-contact discrete element method (MC-DEM) was applied. In contrast to the conventional discrete element method (DEM), MC-DEM interactions between multiple contacts on the same particle are now explicitly taken into account. A new adhesive elastic-plastic multi-contact model invoking neighboring contact interaction was introduced and implemented. The uniaxial compaction of two microcrystalline cellulose grades (Avicel® PH 200 (FMC BioPolymer, Philadelphia, PA, USA) and Pharmacel® 102 (DFE Pharma, Nörten-Hardenberg, Germany) subjected to high confining conditions was studied. The objectives of these simulations were: (1) to investigate the micromechanical behavior; (2) to predict the macroscopic behavior; and (3) to develop a methodology for the calibration of the model parameters needed for the MC-DEM simulations. A two-stage calibration strategy was followed: first, the model parameters were directly measured at the micro-scale (particle level) and second, a meso-scale calibration was established between MC-DEM parameters and compression profiles of the pharmaceutical powders. The new MC-DEM framework could capture the main compressibility characteristics of pharmaceutical materials and could successfully provide predictions on compression profiles at high relative densities.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Granular materials are abundant in nature, and in most industries, either the initial constituents or final products are in granular form during a production or processing stage. Industrial processes and equipment for the handling of bulk solids can only be improved if we can understand, model and predict the material behaviour. The discrete element method (DEM) is a numerical tool well-suited for this purpose and has been used by researchers and engineers to analyse various industrial applications and processes. However, before any bulk scale modelling can be undertaken, the input parameters must be carefully calibrated to obtain accurate results. The calibration of parameter values for non-cohesive materials has reached a level of maturity; however, the calibration of cohesive materials requires more research. This paper details the most prevalent contact models used to model cohesive materials—presented in a consistent notation. Moreover, the significant differences between the models are highlighted to provide a reference for engineers and researchers to select the most appropriate model for a specific application. Finally, a critical review of calibration experiments and methodologies often used for cohesive materials is also presented. This provides a solid basis for DEM practitioners to select the most appropriate calibration methodology for their application and for researchers to extend the current state-of-the-art practices.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The lumpy zone in a blast furnace is composed of piles formed naturally during burden charging. The properties of this zone have significant effects on the blast furnace operation, including heat and mass transfer, chemical reactions and gas flow. The properties of the layers mainly include the angle of repose and porosity distribution. This paper introduces two methods, the Discharging Method and the Lifting Method, to study the influence of the packing method on the angle of repose of the pile. The relationships of the angle of repose and porosity with physical parameters are also investigated. The porosity distribution in the bottom of a pile shows a decreasing trend from the region below the apex to the center. The coordination number of the particles is employed to explain this change. The maximum of the frequency distribution of it was found to show a negative correlation to the static friction coefficient, but becomes insensitive to the parameter as the static friction coefficient increases above 0.6.

Abstract:
Laser sintering is a widely used process for producing complex shapes from particulate materials. However, understanding the complex interaction between the laser and particles is a challenge. This investigation provides new insights into the sintering process by simulating the laser source and the neck growth of particle pairs. First, a multi-physics discrete element method (DEM) framework is developed to incorporate temperature-dependent contact rheological and thermal properties, incorporating heat transfer and neck formation between the particles. Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Micro-scale mechanisms, such as inter-particle and particle-fluid interactions, govern the behaviour of granular systems. While particle-scale simulations provide detailed insights into these interactions, their computational cost is often prohibitive. At a recent Lorentz Center Workshop on “
                    <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://www.lorentzcenter.nl/machine-learning-for-discrete-granular-media.html" ext-link-type="uri">Machine Learning for Discrete Granular Media</jats:ext-link>
                    ”, researchers explored how machine learning approaches can aid the development of constitutive laws and efficient data-driven surrogates for granular materials while also addressing uncertainty quantification. Attended by researchers from both the granular materials (GM) and machine learning (ML) communities, the workshop brought the ML community up to date with GM challenges. This position paper emerged from the workshop discussions. In this position paper, we define granular materials and identify seven key challenges that characterise their distinctive behaviour across various scales and regimes–ranging from gas-like to fluid-like and solid-like. Addressing these challenges is essential for developing robust and efficient models for the digital twinning of granular systems in various industrial applications. To showcase the potential of ML to the GM community, we present classical and emerging machine/deep learning techniques that have been, or could be, applied to granular materials. We reviewed sequence-based learning models for path-dependent constitutive behaviour, followed by encoder-decoder type models for representing high-dimensional data in reduced spaces. We then explore graph neural networks and recent advances in neural operator learning. The latter captures the emerging field evolution of interacting particles via efficient latent space representation. Lastly, we discuss model-order reduction and probabilistic learning techniques for high-dimensional parameterised systems, both of which are crucial for quantifying and incorporating uncertainties arising from physics-based and data-driven models. We present a typical workflow aimed at unifying data structures and modelling pipelines and guiding readers through the selection, training, and deployment of ML surrogates for granular material simulations. Finally, we illustrate the workflow’s practical use with two representative examples, focusing on granular materials in solid-like and fluid-like regimes.
                  </jats:p>

Calibration and validation represent crucial but often-overlooked ingredients in the successful application of discrete element method (DEM) simulations. Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Binder jetting of minimally processed, locally sourced sediments offers a promising route toward sustainable additive manufacturing, but powder spreading of poorly sorted, irregular grains remains underexplored. This study uses high-fidelity Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations to quantify how process parameters govern layer quality when spreading an unrefined sandy silt from the Gypsum Hills, Kansas, USA, with a counter-rotating roller. Twenty-five multi-sphere particle shapes were reconstructed from morphological measurements and used to simulate up to 300,000 interacting grains while systematically varying roller traverse speed, rotational speed, diameter, and layer thickness. Traverse speed and layer thickness emerged as the dominant controls on powder bed density and uniformity: the slowest traverse speed (20 mm/s) produced the highest density (~ 0.50) and lowest variability (~ 0.08), and layer thicknesses ≥ 120 μm were required to avoid jamming and obtain consistent packing. In contrast, roller diameter and rotational speed had only minor influence over the explored ranges. The simulations also revealed percolation-driven segregation, with fine particles preferentially settling beneath coarser grains. Comparison with an idealized spherical powder showed that the silt is intrinsically harder to spread, achieving lower density (0.51 vs. 0.59) and higher variability. These results demonstrate that binder jet processing of unrefined silt is feasible but favors slower spreading and thicker layers that may reduce throughput and resolution, and they provide process design guidelines and particle-scale insight for deploying raw earth feedstocks in sustainable binder jetting.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The spreading behavior of particles has a significant impact on the processing quality of additive manufacturing. Compared with spherical metal material, polymer particles are usually non-spherical in shape. However, the effects of particle shape and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, the spreading process of particles with reconstructed shapes (non-spherical particles decomposed into several spherical shapes by stereo-lithography models) are simulated by integrating spherical particles with the discrete element method. The results show that more cavities form in the spreading beds of particles with reconstructed shapes than those of spheres with blade spreading. Correspondingly, particles with reconstructed shapes have lower packing densities, leading to more uniform packing patterns. Slow propagation speeds of velocity and angular velocity lead to “right-upwards” turning boundaries for particles with reconstructed shapes and “right-downwards” turning boundaries for spherical particles. Moreover, as the blade velocity increases, the packing density decreases. Our calculation results verify each other and are in good agreement with the experiment, providing more details of the behavior of non-spherical particles before additive manufacturing. The comprehensive comparison between polymer non-spherical particles and spherical particles helps develop a reasonable map for the appropriate choice of operating parameters in real processes.
