contexts.context: The excerpt demonstrates calibration using GranuHeap static heaps rather than shear, funnel, density, or compression tests. A cylinder (1.00-cm diameter) lifts at 1.00 cm/s, forming a gravity heap; 16 images are captured over 180°. For each powder mass, 30 runs (10/day across three days) address placement and humidity variability. Binary images are averaged into grayscale, and heap size is quantified by equivalent black pixels, \(NEBP=\sum_p I_p/255\). Optimal masses were 1.50 g Ti6Al4V and 0.62 g Al6061 (equal volume, 0.227 cm³); 480 images form the averaged calibration profile. DEM uses Lethe, velocity-Verlet integration, normal/tangential viscoelastic forces, van der Waals cohesion, and rolling resistance.

contexts.context: The excerpt calibrates DEM Ti6Al4V and Al6061 powders using tangential friction (µt), rolling friction (µr), and surface energy (γ), with fixed restitution 0.9 and material properties. Ti4Al4V used a full-factorial sweep plus refinement: 670 simulations; Al6061 used Latin hypercube sampling: 100 simulations. For Ti6Al4V, equivalent-black-pixel (SAD) calibration gave µt=0.25, µr=0.001, γ=40×10⁻⁵ J/m², whereas angle-of-repose methods produced very different parameter sets. Image-profile SAD reproduced heap morphology better; scalar AOR metrics were non-unique and missed curvature or tip sharpness.

contexts.context: For Ti6Al4V powder, the study compares DEM parameter sets calibrated using different metrics; each metric favors a distinct parameter-space region, demonstrating calibration nonuniqueness. Scalar angle-of-repose/heap-angle metrics cannot capture complex cohesive-powder behavior and may overlook slope curvature and peak sharpness. An image-based sum-of-absolute-differences (SAD) metric distinguishes heap morphologies and local features, producing better agreement with experimental heap profiles and signed-difference maps. Thus, calibration metric choice changes predicted powder behavior, and image-based metrics may better support target-process predictions. The excerpt gives no parameter sensitivities, surrogate/Bayesian method, simulation count, or numerical contact-parameter values.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes global metamodeling for “non-cohesive bulk materials from mining, construction industry and natural materials technology,” including coke, coal, limestone, gravel, sand, woodchips, and corn. It uses spherical particles in LIGGGHTS-PUBLIC 3.8.0 with Hertz–Mindlin no-cohesion contacts and a modified EPSD rolling-friction model. Particle-size distributions are reduced to two parameters using GGS, RRSB, or lognormal functions rather than 10–16 discrete inputs. Across examples, lognormal fitted best (mean \(R^2=0.9935\), MSE \(=0.0010\)), narrowly outperforming RRSB (\(R^2=0.9925\), MSE \(=0.0012\)); GGS performed worse.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are DEM contact parameters (sliding friction, rolling friction, JKR or SJKR surface energy, restitution, Young's modulus) calibrated for cohesive powders by simulating standard characterization tests: shear cells (Jenike, Schulze ring shear, FT4 rotational shear), FT4 dynamic flow (basic flowability energy), angle of repose (fixed funnel, rotating drum, lifting cylinder), Hall and Carney funnel discharge, bulk and tapped density, and uniaxial compression? Which tests are sensitive to which parameters, which parameter combinations are not identifiable from one test, and which combinations of tests break the degeneracy? Which surrogate and Bayesian methods are used (GrainLearning sequential Monte Carlo, Gaussian-process emulators, Kriging, polynomial chaos, neural-network surrogates, MCMC, approximate Bayesian computation, design of experiments), with how many simulations? Give quantitative examples for metal additive-manufacturing powders, salts and pharmaceutical powders.

contexts.context: Rackl and Hanley calibrate LIGGGHTS using Hertz–Mindlin contact plus elastic-plastic spring-dashpot rolling friction. Seven factors include particle/wall Young’s modulus, static and rolling friction, particle density, and a Rayleigh-time-step weighting factor; simulations use one-quarter of the critical timestep, Eq. (1), with timestep stability explicitly penalized. Latin-hypercube sampling generated 5,000 designs per calibration factor, followed by Kriging. Responses were bulk density and angle of repose, simulated by pouring 5-mm particles into a 100-mm cylinder, then lifting it at 10 mm/s. Target glass-bead values were 1,500 kg/m³ and 22°. Distinct parameter sets produced similar outcomes, demonstrating non-identifiability and parameter interactions.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. contexts.context: Rackl and Hanley (2016) propose automated DEM calibration using Latin-hypercube design and Kriging rather than trial-and-error. They calibrate spherical glass beads against angle of repose and bulk density, including particle density, Young’s modulus, static friction, rolling friction, and simulation time-step. Kriging closely reproduced DEM responses, while calibrated solutions were non-unique: different parameter combinations yielded similar bulk behavior. Static and rolling friction showed no correlation, contradicting a common assumption. Including the Rayleigh time-step produced substantially larger, computationally efficient time steps without degrading calibration. The excerpt does not address cohesive powders, JKR/SJKR, shear cells, or Bayesian methods.

contexts.context: A DEM calibration study used 546 shear-cell and 81 static angle-of-repose simulations, varying sliding/rolling friction (0.1–1.0), restitution (0.5–0.9), particle density (2500–3500 kg/m³), and cohesion-related diameter parameters. Multilayer perceptrons (70% training, 15% validation, remainder testing) emulated shear-cell outputs (particle-wall friction, shear friction, bulk density) and angle of repose; a 15-neuron ANN achieved \(R^2=0.96\). It evaluated 6,250,000 parameter combinations virtually, retaining combinations whose three shear-cell quantities and AoR each matched experiments within 5%. This demonstrates combining shear and AoR tests to constrain parameter degeneracy.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes DEM parameter identification using macroscopic tests because microscopic measurements are impractical and rolling friction is empirical. A feed-forward ANN, trained by back-propagation on a database of DEM simulations spanning contact parameters and particle-size distributions, maps inputs to bulk outputs and identifies parameter sets matching experiments. It emphasizes nonuniqueness: parameters fitting angle of repose may fail shear tests, while brute-force calibration is computationally expensive. Demonstration used particle radii mean 0.732 mm, SD 0.410 mm, Young’s modulus 10 MPa, Poisson ratio 0.400, and timestep \(10^{-6}\) s.

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes that surrogate accuracy depends strongly on sampling. One-shot full-factorial/LHS designs are unsuitable without prior knowledge; sequential space-filling designs are preferred. It compares Halton and Sobol quasi-random sequences, FSSF-f, and MIPT using 100 points in 2D and 10D, repeated 10 times. FSSF-f produced the highest minimum intersite distance (MID) and lowest cover measure (COV), while MIPT degraded in 10D. For metamodels, global, interpretable, introspective, and extrapolative behavior is required; local linear/quadratic models are excluded. The selected approach is symbolic regression, searching mathematical expressions for accurate, simple relationships.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes global DEM metamodel calibration using a scalable shear-box discharge test. Input ranges include particle/wall Young’s modulus \(5\times10^6\!-\!5\times10^8\) Pa, restitution 0.05–0.95, sliding/rolling friction 0–1, density 250–3000 kg/m³, and PSD \(d_{50}=0.40\!-\!25.6\) mm. Several hundred simulations are required for training. Geometry is scaled so the smallest box dimension equals \(10d_{\max}\); timestep is \(\Delta t=0.25T_R\). Experiments should be small, scale-invariant, robust, and avoid bridging. Sampling may be one-shot (factorial, Latin hypercube) or sequential.

contexts.context: Benvenuti et al. identify DEM parameters using ANN surrogates trained on random DEM simulations of angle-of-repose (AoR) and Schulze shear-cell (SSC) tests. Inputs included sliding friction \(\mu_s\), rolling friction \(\mu_r\), restitution (COR), particle density, and cylinder/particle-size ratio; rolling torque follows \(T_{r,\max}=\mu_rR_rF_n\), while \(F_t\le\mu_sF_n\). SSC simulations replicated 12 normal-stress/load conditions and produced bulk density, pre-shear friction, shear friction, and AoR. Data were split 70% training/30% testing; ANN predictions were compared with Bayesian linear and Gaussian nonlinear regression. Valid parameter sets were found separately for AoR and SSC, then combined for reliability.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not report numerical calibrated DEM parameter values for Ti-6Al-4V or for other metal AM powders such as 316L, AlSi10Mg, or IN718. In particular, it provides no tabulated values for sliding friction, rolling friction, cohesion or surface energy, or restitution coefficient. It does state that calibration-metric choice strongly affects the selected DEM parameter region: distinct metrics favor different parameter combinations and therefore produce different predicted powder behavior. The proposed image-based SAD metric is reported to provide more consistent agreement between experimental and simulated heap profiles than scalar angle-of-repose (AOR) metrics. It is more sensitive to heap morphology, including local slope curvature and peak sharpness, which scalar AOR approaches may miss. Thus, the excerpt supports a qualitative conclusion that AOR and heap morphology are sensitive to the combined DEM parameter set and to the calibration metric, but it does not quantify parameter-by-parameter sensitivity or discuss powder spreading sensitivity. The references mention studies on Ti-alloy and powder-spreading simulations, but their numerical parameter values and sensitivity results are not included in the supplied pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report Sobol sensitivity indices and does not concern an oedometer compression test; it analyzes a DEM virtual cone penetration test. Therefore, it cannot establish which parameter has the largest Sobol index or whether Young’s modulus is the most significant parameter for oedometer compression. It does provide qualitative sensitivity information for penetration energy density Ez. Increasing particle Young’s modulus Ep decreases Ez, because stiffer particles deform less, reducing contact area and cohesive forces. Increasing the sliding friction coefficient μ increases Ez monotonically. Rolling friction μr is described as relatively unimportant for the investigated case, contributing only a few kPa compared with typical sample strengths of a few MPa, although it can matter at low sliding friction where particle interlocking controls strength. Cohesion energy density Ω has a large, non-monotonic influence, with peak strength reported near Ω ≈ 80 MPa and a decrease beyond that associated with crack formation. The authors introduce a parameter sensitivity matrix and evaluate 81 simulations, but the excerpt does not provide Sobol indices or numerical sensitivity values for Ep, μr, or μ. Results from this cone-penetration analysis should not be transferred directly to oedometer compression.

Question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are DEM contact parameters (sliding friction, rolling friction, JKR or SJKR surface energy, restitution, Young's modulus) calibrated for cohesive powders by simulating standard characterization tests: shear cells (Jenike, Schulze ring shear, FT4 rotational shear), FT4 dynamic flow (basic flowability energy), angle of repose (fixed funnel, rotating drum, lifting cylinder), Hall and Carney funnel discharge, bulk and tapped density, and uniaxial compression? Which tests are sensitive to which parameters, which parameter combinations are not identifiable from one test, and which combinations of tests break the degeneracy? Which surrogate and Bayesian methods are used (GrainLearning sequential Monte Carlo, Gaussian-process emulators, Kriging, polynomial chaos, neural-network surrogates, MCMC, approximate Bayesian computation, design of experiments), with how many simulations? Give quantitative examples for metal additive-manufacturing powders, salts and pharmaceutical powders.

## DEM Contact Parameter Calibration for Cohesive Powders: Tests, Sensitivity, Identifiability, and Surrogate/Bayesian Methods

### 1. Overview of Calibration Strategy

DEM calibration for cohesive powders typically follows a staged approach. First, non-cohesive parameters (sliding friction, rolling friction, restitution, Young's modulus) are calibrated using flow-property and bench-scale tests; then cohesive parameters (surface energy, cohesion energy density) are introduced while keeping the dry parameters fixed (coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 32-34). Restitution is often obtained from particle drop tests, particle–wall sliding friction from Jenike direct-shear or inclined-wall tests, and Young's modulus from literature or nano-indentation rather than from bulk flow tests (coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 32-34). This staged strategy is necessary because the parameter space is high-dimensional and individual tests cannot uniquely resolve all parameters simultaneously.

### 2. Which Tests Are Sensitive to Which Parameters

The following table synthesizes sensitivity findings from multiple studies employing factorial designs, Sobol indices, and regression analyses.

| DEM contact parameter | Angle of repose / heap | Shear cell (Jenike, Schulze, FT4 shear) | FT4-like dynamic yield / blade flow | Oedometer / bulk density | Powder spreading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sliding friction, μs** | **High** for free-flowing powders; **low–moderate** for cohesive powders, where rolling resistance and cohesion can dominate. Different μs–μr–γ combinations can reproduce the same angle. (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 12-15) | **High** for pre-shear and critical-state stress; often the dominant pre-shear parameter, but sensitivity can saturate above μs ≈ 0.4. (chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 3-5, chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 5-6, karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 33-37) | **Moderate**; changing sliding friction produced about an 18.8% change in dynamic yield strength in one pharmaceutical-powder study. (karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 33-37) | **High for loose packing/bulk porosity**, because μs and μr jointly control rearrangement; generally below Young’s modulus for force–displacement response in an oedometer. (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2, jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 1-2, jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 3-5) | **Moderate–high**: controls shearing beneath the recoater and particle–substrate drag, but can trade off against rolling resistance and cohesion. A Ti-6Al-4V example used μpp = 0.185, μspreader = 0.12 and μsubstrate = 0.25. (zhang2017machinelearningenabled pages 4-7, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 9-12) |
| **Rolling friction, μr** | **High**, especially for cohesive or spherical-particle models; commonly compensates for unresolved angularity/roughness and was the strongest AoR factor for cohesive lactose. (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2) | **Moderate–high** when particle rotation and shape interlocking matter; raising μr increased simulated critical-state stress from 1008 to 1183 Pa in one study. (karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 33-37) | **Moderate–high**; increasing μr caused about a 37% increase in dynamic yield strength, with the strongest response up to μr ≈ 0.3. (karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 33-37) | **High for packing/porosity** but **low relative to Young’s modulus for oedometer stiffness**. μs and μr are jointly influential and cannot usually be separated using density alone. (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2, jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 1-2) | **Moderate–high**: governs particle rotation, apparent angularity and bed packing; however, it is confounded with μs and γ in heap-based calibration. (gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 9-12, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 12-15) |
| **JKR/SJKR surface energy, γ, or cohesion-energy density** | **High for cohesive powders**, including heap curvature, clumping, collapse onset and no-flow/bridging; a scalar AoR alone cannot uniquely separate cohesion from friction. (roessler2019demparametercalibration pages 2-3, roessler2019demparametercalibration pages 1-2, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 9-12) | **High**: surface energy significantly affects pre-shear stress and was the most important factor for incipient-flow stress in a 32-run ring-shear design. (chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 3-5, chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 5-6) | **Very high**: increasing surface energy raised dynamic yield strength from 495 to 1853 Pa, a 274.3% increase, in the cited pharmaceutical example. (karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 33-37) | **Moderate** for loose/cohesive packing, agglomeration and consolidation history; a simple elastic JKR/SJKR model is inadequate for strong irreversible compaction. (coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 28-30, roessler2019demparametercalibration pages 2-3) | **Very high for fine AM powders**: cohesion lowers mean layer packing and increases roughness/heterogeneity; for ≈30 μm metal particles, adhesion can exceed gravity by roughly an order of magnitude. (meier2021physics‐basedmodelingand pages 2-4) |
| **Young’s modulus / contact stiffness, E** | **Low** over many reduced-stiffness ranges, provided overlaps remain small; it can become relevant when cohesion depends on contact area. (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 2-3, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2) | **Low for pre-shear**, but **moderate–high for incipient flow at high cohesion**; tested range 0.13–1.3 GPa. (chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 3-5, chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 5-6) | **Moderate** in the cited yield-strength study, where changing shear stiffness altered dynamic yield strength by about 19.2%; effects are model- and stress-dependent. (karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 33-37) | **Very high for oedometer/uniaxial force–displacement response** and the dominant Sobol-sensitive parameter in the investigated oedometer domain; density alone is much less diagnostic of E. (jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 1-2, jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 3-5) | **Low–moderate** for quasi-static spreading if reduced safely; mainly controls overlap, collision/contact duration and computational time rather than final layer morphology. (gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 9-12, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 12-15) |
| **Restitution, e** | **Low–negligible** for the final static heap, though it affects transient avalanching and settling time. (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2) | **Negligible for mean pre-shear/incipient stress** in the cited screening study, but **moderate for stress-fluctuation amplitude**. (chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 3-5, chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 5-6) | **Negligible–low** under slow dense flow; changing e produced only about a 4.6% dynamic-yield-strength change in one study. (karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 33-37) | **Low** for quasi-static density/compression after settling; principally affects collision damping rather than equilibrium stiffness. (jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 1-2, jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 3-5) | **Low–moderate**: more relevant at high recoater speed or impact-dominated deposition than in slow, dense spreading; reported AM studies often fix e rather than calibrate it. (gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 12-15, zhang2017machinelearningenabled pages 4-7) |


*Table: Qualitative sensitivity of five common DEM contact parameters across standard powder tests and AM spreading. Ratings are regime-dependent: quasi-static versus dynamic response, cohesive versus free-flowing behavior, and the chosen contact model can change the ranking.*

**Key findings by test type:**

**Shear cells (Schulze ring shear, FT4 rotational shear).** In a 32-run, five-factor full-factorial DEM screening of the Schulze ring shear test, particle sliding friction was the dominant factor for pre-shear stress, while surface energy was the most important factor for incipient-flow (yield) stress (chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 3-5, chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 5-6). Young's modulus became statistically significant for incipient flow at high cohesion, but restitution and Poisson's ratio were non-significant for mean stress (chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 5-6). Rolling friction increased critical-state stress from 1008 to 1183 Pa in a parallel-plate shear-cell study, while sliding friction effects saturated above approximately 0.4 (karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 33-37).

**FT4 dynamic flow / dynamic yield strength (DYS).** Surface energy (cohesion) is overwhelmingly dominant: increasing it from baseline raised DYS by 274.3% (495 → 1853 Pa), followed by rolling friction at 37.0%, shear modulus at −19.2%, sliding friction at −18.8%, and restitution at only −4.6% (karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 33-37).

**Angle of repose (fixed funnel, lifting cylinder, rotating drum).** For free-flowing powders, static friction is the critical parameter with a positive power-law dependence on AoR (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2). For cohesive powders, rolling friction has a substantial impact while static friction and particle size play minor roles (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2). Cohesion controls heap curvature, clumping, and collapse onset, but a scalar AoR cannot uniquely separate cohesion from friction (roessler2019demparametercalibration pages 2-3, roessler2019demparametercalibration pages 1-2, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 1-3). Different AoR measurement methods (height/radius ratio, full-slope regression, half-slope regression) yield different "best" parameter sets—for Ti6Al4V powder, the image-based SAD metric favored low μs, low μr, high γ, while the height/radius AoR method favored high μs, high μr, low γ (gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 12-15).

**Oedometer / uniaxial compression / bulk density.** Young's modulus is the most significant parameter for the oedometer force–displacement response, as confirmed by Sobol sensitivity analysis, while rolling friction dominates the pile experiment (jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 1-2, jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 3-5). For loose packing porosity, both static and rolling friction coefficients are highly influential (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2).

**Powder spreading in AM.** For fine metal powders (~30 μm), adhesive forces exceed gravity by roughly an order of magnitude, making cohesion/surface energy the dominant parameter controlling mean packing fraction and surface roughness (meier2021physics‐basedmodelingand pages 2-4). Sliding friction controls particle–substrate and particle–recoater interactions (zhang2017machinelearningenabled pages 4-7).

### 3. Parameter Degeneracy and Identifiability

A central finding across the literature is that **no single test can uniquely identify all DEM contact parameters**. Specific non-identifiability issues include:

- **Angle of repose alone** produces a large solution manifold: different combinations of μs, μr, and γ yield the same scalar AoR (gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 1-3, rackl2017amethodicalcalibration pages 1-2). Rackl and Hanley showed that substantially different parameter sets produce similar AoR and bulk density simultaneously, and found no correlation between static and rolling friction despite this sometimes being assumed (rackl2017amethodicalcalibration pages 1-2). Gaboriault et al. demonstrated that four different AoR measurement methods selected four distinct parameter clusters for the same Ti6Al4V powder (gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 12-15).

- **Sliding and rolling friction** are confounded in most flow tests because both resist relative particle motion. In the El-Kassem study, the same AoR could be achieved with various μs–μr combinations (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2). Coetzee and Scheffler found that slump and hopper tests required different rolling-friction values for the same sliding friction, indicating poor transferability (coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 32-34).

- **Cohesion and friction** are degenerate in heap tests: a more cohesive powder with lower friction can produce the same pile geometry as a less cohesive powder with higher friction (roessler2019demparametercalibration pages 2-3, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 1-3).

- **Young's modulus** is poorly constrained by flow tests (AoR, funnel discharge) since reducing it over several orders of magnitude has negligible effect on flowability for free-flowing materials (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 2-3), but it dominates the oedometer response (jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 1-2, jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 3-5).

**Breaking the degeneracy** requires combining tests that activate different physical mechanisms. The recommended multi-test strategies from the literature include:

- **Shear cell + angle of repose + bulk density**: The shear cell constrains friction and surface energy under controlled consolidation stress; AoR constrains friction and cohesion under gravity flow; bulk density constrains packing and indirectly Young's modulus (coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 28-30, coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 32-34).

- **DYS or drop test for cohesion + shear cell for friction**: Karkala's approach uses dynamic yield strength simulations to calibrate JKR surface energy independently, then parallel-plate shear simulations to calibrate sliding and rolling friction (karkala2021analysisofpowder pages 24-28).

- **Full-field heap morphology instead of scalar AoR**: Gaboriault et al.'s pixel-based SAD metric better constrains the parameter space than any single AoR definition by capturing slope curvature, peak sharpness, and concavity (gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 1-3, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 12-15).

- **Oedometer for stiffness + pile for friction**: Since Young's modulus dominates the oedometer while rolling friction dominates the pile, combining these two tests separates these otherwise-confounded parameters (jahn2023onthesensitivity pages 3-5).

### 4. Surrogate and Bayesian Calibration Methods

| Method | Algorithm details | Reported / typical DEM simulation budget | Key references | Notes / advantages |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| **GrainLearning sequential Monte Carlo (SMC/SQMC)** | Runs an ensemble of parameter samples, weights trajectories by agreement with time-series observations, recursively updates the posterior, and resamples from a fitted Gaussian-mixture/variational distribution. Surrogates such as recurrent neural networks may replace DEM evaluations. | No universal count; cost is **ensemble size × calibration rounds**. In Cheng’s SQMC example, posterior changes became small after about **60 data-assimilation steps**, but these are observation increments—not 60 independent DEM runs. | Cheng et al.; GrainLearning toolbox (cheng2024grainlearningabayesian pages 1-3, cheng2024grainlearningabayesian pages 3-4, cheng2018probabilisticcalibrationof pages 8-11, cheng2018probabilisticcalibrationof pages 16-18) | Produces posterior distributions and parameter correlations rather than a single optimum. Especially useful for path-dependent dosing/shear curves, but requires monitoring effective sample size, particle impoverishment, model discrepancy, and stochastic DEM variance. |
| **Kriging / Gaussian-process surrogate with Latin-hypercube sampling** | Space-filling LHS generates DEM training points; a Kriging/GP emulator maps parameters to multiple bulk responses and is searched for matching parameter sets. Predictive variance can guide adaptive sampling. | Problem-dependent. Rackl and Hanley calibrated **7 factors** against angle of repose and bulk density; the cited evidence does not give the exact run count. Conventional calibration commonly reaches **hundreds to thousands** of runs without an efficient surrogate. | Rackl & Hanley; Richter & Will (richter2021introducingmetamodelbasedglobal pages 1-3, rackl2017amethodicalcalibration pages 1-2, rackl2017amethodicalcalibration pages 2-3) | Well suited to roughly 3–8 continuous parameters and expensive DEM. Gives uncertainty estimates and exposes solution manifolds; Rackl found multiple parameter combinations with similar responses and no assumed μs–μr correlation. |
| **Artificial-neural-network surrogate** | Feed-forward ANN learns the mapping from DEM inputs to shear-cell and heap outputs; millions of candidate parameter combinations are then screened inexpensively through the trained network. | Benvenuti et al.: **546 shear-cell + 81 angle-of-repose simulations = 627 DEM runs**; the trained ANN subsequently screened **6,250,000** parameter combinations. | Benvenuti, Kloss & Pirker (benvenuti2015demparameteridentification pages 1-2, benvenuti2015demparameteridentification pages 2-3, benvenuti2015demparameteridentification pages 3-4) | Handles nonlinear, multi-output responses and makes exhaustive post-training searches cheap. Requires enough training/validation data, provides less transparent uncertainty than a GP, and can extrapolate unreliably outside the training domain. |
| **Metamodel-Based Global Calibration (MBGC; symbolic regression)** | A reusable, domain-wide surrogate is trained once across contact parameters, density, and a parameterized PSD. Symbolic regression/genetic programming seeks an interpretable global equation; later materials are calibrated without new DEM runs if they remain inside the trained domain. | **Several hundred DEM simulations** for one-time global training; subsequent calibrations can use surrogate predictions alone. | Richter & Will (richter2021introducingmetamodelbasedglobal pages 5-7, richter2021introducingmetamodelbasedglobal pages 3-5, richter2021introducingmetamodelbasedglobal pages 1-3, richter2021introducingmetamodelbasedglobal pages 7-9, richter2021introducingmetamodelbasedglobal pages 9-12) | Amortizes cost over many powders and yields interpretable relationships. Transfer is valid only for the same contact model, test geometry, particle representation, and covered material/PSD domain. |
| **Response-surface methodology / D-optimal design of experiments** | A screening or optimized design fits linear/quadratic regression with interactions; insignificant factors are removed and the response surface is optimized or inverted. | El-Kassem et al.: **40 runs** for free-flowing lactose and **53 runs** for cohesive lactose across five or six inputs. Chen et al.: **32 simulations** for a five-factor, two-level ring-shear screening design, followed by an augmented response-surface stage. | El-Kassem et al.; Chen, Pei & Elliott (chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 3-5, chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 5-6, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 9-10, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 11-13) | Efficient for screening and smooth, low-order responses; directly estimates interactions and sensitivity. Quadratic surfaces may miss discontinuities such as jamming, intermittent no-flow, avalanches, or regime changes. |
| **Evolutionary optimization (e.g., ACCES)** | Population-based evolutionary search automatically launches simulations, evaluates multiple comparators, mutates/recombines candidates, and iterates toward lower discrepancy; it can be coupled to metamodels and parallel execution. | No fixed budget in the cited evidence. Brute-force comparison shows the motivation: a 10-point grid needs **100 runs for 2 parameters** but about **1,000,000 for 6 parameters**. | Nicuşan et al. (nicusan2025accesnoninvasivesimulation pages 2-4) | Robust to noisy, non-smooth and multimodal objectives and easy to parallelize. Usually returns optima rather than a Bayesian posterior unless embedded in a probabilistic workflow; can still consume many DEM runs. |
| **Full-factorial / dense parametric sweep** | Evaluates every selected parameter-level combination, optionally followed by local refinement around the best candidates. It is simple and unbiased by a surrogate form but scales exponentially with dimension. | Chen ring-shear screening: **2⁵ = 32 runs**. Gaboriault et al.: **670 Ti6Al4V runs** using factorial sweep plus refinement and **100 Al6061 runs** using LHS. | Chen, Pei & Elliott; Gaboriault et al. (chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 5-6, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 12-15) | Provides clear interaction maps and a strong benchmark in low dimension. Becomes impractical beyond a few parameters; Gaboriault’s results also showed that different heap metrics select substantially different μs–μr–γ optima. |


*Table: Comparison of Bayesian, surrogate, optimization, and design-of-experiments strategies for DEM calibration, including reported simulation budgets. Counts are study-specific and should not be treated as universal sample-size requirements.*

**GrainLearning (Sequential Monte Carlo / SQMC).** This Bayesian toolbox uses iterative importance sampling: an ensemble of DEM parameter samples is weighted by agreement with time-series observations (e.g., stress–strain curves), the posterior is recursively updated via Bayes' rule, and a Gaussian-mixture model is fitted to resample for the next iteration (cheng2024grainlearningabayesian pages 1-3, cheng2024grainlearningabayesian pages 3-4). In Cheng et al.'s triaxial-compression calibration of granular soils in a five-dimensional parameter space, posterior distributions stabilized after approximately 60 data-assimilation steps (cheng2018probabilisticcalibrationof pages 8-11). GrainLearning can substitute recurrent neural networks for the DEM simulator, reducing cost by "several orders of magnitude" (cheng2024grainlearningabayesian pages 3-4). The method produces posterior distributions and parameter correlations rather than single optima (cheng2018probabilisticcalibrationof pages 16-18).

**Kriging / Gaussian-process emulators.** Rackl and Hanley used Latin-hypercube sampling to generate DEM training data for a seven-parameter calibration (particle density, Young's modulus, μs,pp, μs,pw, μr,pp, μr,pw, time-step weighting) against AoR and bulk density for glass beads. The Kriging meta-models showed "excellent correlation" with DEM responses (rackl2017amethodicalcalibration pages 1-2, rackl2017amethodicalcalibration pages 2-3). Richter and Will also list Kriging and Gaussian-process models among effective surrogate types, alongside neural networks (richter2021introducingmetamodelbasedglobal pages 3-5).

**Artificial neural networks.** Benvenuti et al. trained a feed-forward ANN on 546 shear-cell and 81 AoR DEM simulations (627 total) for iron-ore sinter fines with four varied parameters (μs, μr, COR, ρp). The trained ANN then screened 6,250,000 parameter combinations to identify sets matching experimental bulk density, internal friction, and AoR within 5% (benvenuti2015demparameteridentification pages 1-2, benvenuti2015demparameteridentification pages 2-3, benvenuti2015demparameteridentification pages 3-4). The ANN achieved R² = 0.96 with 15 hidden neurons (benvenuti2015demparameteridentification pages 3-4).

**Metamodel-Based Global Calibration (MBGC).** Richter and Will trained a reusable symbolic-regression surrogate across a 12-dimensional parameter space (including parameterized PSD) using "several hundred" DEM simulations. Once trained, the metamodel enables instant calibration for new materials within the same domain without additional DEM runs (richter2021introducingmetamodelbasedglobal pages 5-7, richter2021introducingmetamodelbasedglobal pages 3-5, richter2021introducingmetamodelbasedglobal pages 1-3).

**Response Surface Methodology / D-optimal DoE.** El-Kassem et al. used quadratic D-optimal designs with 40 runs (free-flowing lactose, 5 parameters) and 53 runs (cohesive lactose, 6 parameters including SJKR cohesion energy density) to build multivariate regression models with adjusted R² = 0.954 for AoR (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 10-11, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 9-10). Chen et al. used 32 simulations for a five-factor screening of the ring shear cell, followed by response-surface augmentation (chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 3-5, chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 5-6).

**Evolutionary algorithms (ACCES).** Nicuşan et al. describe population-based evolutionary optimization for DEM calibration, noting that brute-force grid search requires ~100 simulations for 2 parameters but ~10⁶ for 6 parameters, motivating surrogate-assisted approaches (nicusan2025accesnoninvasivesimulation pages 2-4).

**Metal AM powders.** For Ti6Al4V (D5–D95 = 45–111 μm), full-field heap calibration using 670 DEM simulations yielded μs = 0.25, μr = 0.001, γ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ J/m², e = 0.9, Y = 26.25 MPa (gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 9-12, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 12-15). For Al6061 (D5–D95 = 18–50 μm), 100 LHS simulations yielded μs = 0.68, μr = 0.093, γ = 5.8 × 10⁻⁵ J/m² (gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 9-12, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 12-15). These results highlight that even within metal AM powders, calibrated parameters vary substantially between alloys and particle sizes. Meier et al. report an effective surface energy of γ = 0.1 mJ/m² for fine metal AM powder calibrated via static AoR, noting that for ~30 μm particles, adhesive forces already exceed gravity by an order of magnitude (meier2021physics‐basedmodelingand pages 2-4). Zhang et al. report μpp = 0.185 and e = 0.8 for Ti-6Al-4V DEM spreading simulations (zhang2017machinelearningenabled pages 4-7).

**Pharmaceutical powders.** For free-flowing lactose (SpheroLac 100, D[3,4] = 115 μm, AoR = 33°), the D-optimal DoE varied μs over 0.10–0.85, μr over 0.05–0.75, e over 0.051–0.60, and Y over 0.026–2.6 GPa across 40 simulations (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 10-11, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 9-10). For cohesive lactose (InhaLac 251, D[3,4] = 53.4 μm, AoR = 40°), SJKR cohesion energy density was varied over 30,000–70,000 J/m³ across 53 simulations, with rolling friction showing the strongest AoR effect in the cohesive regime (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 9-10, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 11-13). In ring-shear DEM of cohesive lactose, Chen et al. found that particle friction (0.1–0.8) and surface energy (10⁻⁴–0.1 J/m²) were highly significant for shear stress, while restitution and Poisson's ratio were non-significant (chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 3-5, chen2022a“sequentialdesign pages 5-6).

**Iron ore and industrial powders.** Benvenuti et al. calibrated iron-ore sinter fines using combined shear-cell and AoR data, training ANNs on 627 DEM simulations with μs ∈ [0.4, 0.8], μr ∈ [0.4, 0.8], COR ∈ [0.5, 0.9], and ρp ∈ [2500, 3500] kg/m³. Valid parameter combinations were identified by requiring all four bulk responses (pre-shear friction, shear friction, bulk density, and AoR) to match experiments within 5% (benvenuti2015demparameteridentification pages 1-2, benvenuti2015demparameteridentification pages 2-3, benvenuti2015demparameteridentification pages 3-4).

### 6. Implications for Auger Dosing and Powder-Bed AM Spreadability

For the context of an auger doser calibration targeting simulation-based Bayesian inference, several practical conclusions emerge. The "dosing fingerprint" (mass/revolution, tap-freed mass, afterflow time constant, no-flow fraction) provides multi-modal calibration targets analogous to combining AoR, shear, and dynamic tests. Since angle of repose alone is demonstrably non-unique for cohesive powders (gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 1-3, gaboriault2026fromangleof pages 12-15), using multiple dosing observables simultaneously should help break the μs–μr–γ degeneracy. The LIGGGHTS Hertz-Mindlin + SJKR + constant-directional-torque rolling friction model used in the user's 105 mg/rev salt simulation is consistent with the contact models employed in many of the cited calibration studies (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 5-6, roessler2019demparametercalibration pages 2-3). For computationally expensive simulations (26–30 CPU-minutes per revolution), surrogate-assisted Bayesian methods such as GrainLearning SMC or GP-emulator-based calibration are strongly recommended over brute-force parameter sweeps, as they can achieve convergence with O(10²) rather than O(10⁴–10⁶) simulations (cheng2024grainlearningabayesian pages 1-3, nicusan2025accesnoninvasivesimulation pages 2-4, rackl2017amethodicalcalibration pages 1-2).

For anticipating powder-bed spreadability from calibrated DEM parameters, cohesion (surface energy) is the most critical parameter: for fine metal powders, adhesion forces dominate gravity and control both packing fraction and surface roughness of spread layers (meier2021physics‐basedmodelingand pages 2-4). Parameters calibrated against dosing or heap tests should be validated against independent spreading experiments before predictive use in AM process simulation, since parameter transferability between different test geometries and stress states is not guaranteed (coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 32-34, coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 28-30).

Gives uncertainty estimates and exposes solution manifolds; Rackl found multiple parameter combinations with similar responses and no assumed μs–μr correlation. |
| **Artificial-neural-network surrogate** | Feed-forward ANN learns the mapping from DEM inputs to shear-cell and heap outputs; millions of candidate parameter combinations are then screened inexpensively through the trained network. | Benvenuti et al.: **546 shear-cell + 81 angle-of-repose simulations = 627 DEM runs**; the trained ANN subsequently screened **6,250,000** parameter combinations. | Benvenuti, Kloss & Pirker (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040) | Handles nonlinear, multi-output responses and makes exhaustive post-training searches cheap. Requires enough training/validation data, provides less transparent uncertainty than a GP, and can extrapolate unreliably outside the training domain. |
| **Metamodel-Based Global Calibration (MBGC; symbolic regression)** | A reusable, domain-wide surrogate is trained once across contact parameters, density, and a parameterized PSD. Symbolic regression/genetic programming seeks an interpretable global equation; later materials are calibrated without new DEM runs if they remain inside the trained domain. | **Several hundred DEM simulations** for one-time global training; subsequent calibrations can use surrogate predictions alone. | Richter & Will (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035) | Amortizes cost over many powders and yields interpretable relationships. Transfer is valid only for the same contact model, test geometry, particle representation, and covered material/PSD domain. |
| **Response-surface methodology / D-optimal design of experiments** | A screening or optimized design fits linear/quadratic regression with interactions; insignificant factors are removed and the response surface is optimized or inverted. | El-Kassem et al.: **40 runs** for free-flowing lactose and **53 runs** for cohesive lactose across five or six inputs. Chen et al.: **32 simulations** for a five-factor, two-level ring-shear screening design, followed by an augmented response-surface stage. | El-Kassem et al.; Chen, Pei & Elliott (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Efficient for screening and smooth, low-order responses; directly estimates interactions and sensitivity. Quadratic surfaces may miss discontinuities such as jamming, intermittent no-flow, avalanches, or regime changes. |
| **Evolutionary optimization (e.g., ACCES)** | Population-based evolutionary search automatically launches simulations, evaluates multiple comparators, mutates/recombines candidates, and iterates toward lower discrepancy; it can be coupled to metamodels and parallel execution. | No fixed budget in the cited evidence. Brute-force comparison shows the motivation: a 10-point grid needs **100 runs for 2 parameters** but about **1,000,000 for 6 parameters**. | Nicuşan et al. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000028) | Robust to noisy, non-smooth and multimodal objectives and easy to parallelize. Usually returns optima rather than a Bayesian posterior unless embedded in a probabilistic workflow; can still consume many DEM runs. |
| **Full-factorial / dense parametric sweep** | Evaluates every selected parameter-level combination, optionally followed by local refinement around the best candidates. It is simple and unbiased by a surrogate form but scales exponentially with dimension. | Chen ring-shear screening: **2⁵ = 32 runs**. Gaboriault et al.: **670 Ti6Al4V runs** using factorial sweep plus refinement and **100 Al6061 runs** using LHS. | Chen, Pei & Elliott; Gaboriault et al. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000026) | Provides clear interaction maps and a strong benchmark in low dimension. Becomes impractical beyond a few parameters; Gaboriault’s results also showed that different heap metrics select substantially different μs–μr–γ optima. |


*Table: Comparison of Bayesian, surrogate, optimization, and design-of-experiments strategies for DEM calibration, including reported simulation budgets. Counts are study-specific and should not be treated as universal sample-size requirements.*

info.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are DEM contact parameters (sliding friction, rolling friction, JKR or SJKR surface energy, restitution, Young's modulus) calibrated for cohesive powders by simulating standard characterization tests: shear cells (Jenike, Schulze ring shear, FT4 rotational shear), FT4 dynamic flow (basic flowability energy), angle of repose (fixed funnel, rotating drum, lifting cylinder), Hall and Carney funnel discharge, bulk and tapped density, and uniaxial compression? Which tests are sensitive to which parameters, which parameter combinations are not identifiable from one test, and which combinations of tests break the degeneracy? Which surrogate and Bayesian methods are used (GrainLearning sequential Monte Carlo, Gaussian-process emulators, Kriging, polynomial chaos, neural-network surrogates, MCMC, approximate Bayesian computation, design of experiments), with how many simulations? Give quantitative examples for metal additive-manufacturing powders, salts and pharmaceutical powders.
